The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6452. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying size, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using their AC adapters, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with over five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-rated starting-watts power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

With the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

But everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

One downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no issues at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

With its tremendous capacity, the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 is truly capable of providing basic whole-home backup without gas or solar panels. Our test rig came with one expansion battery, raising its capacity to 8,096 watt-hours.

It was also the most efficient power station we tested, outputting 97 percent of its listed power capacity, so most of that energy goes into your appliances, rather than internal functions. We were able to run a space heater pulling a consistent 1,300 watts for nearly 6 hours.

Similar to other large portable power stations, the Pro Delta 3 has a highly expandable modular design, allowing you to add up to two batteries to increase its storage capacity. By adding battery packs and a second power station, it’s possible to create a system with a combined 48-kilowatt-hour capacity.

The Delta Pro 3 produces a max output of 4,000 watts, or up to 6,000 watts through its X-Boost feature, which automatically turns on when your wattage demand exceeds 4,000 watts. This is especially useful for large appliances that require a lot of power when you first turn them on or when under heavy load, such as window air conditioning units and power tools. We pushed it well above 5,000 watts with no noticeable lags by simultaneously operating an air fryer, toaster, and a space heater while making intermittent cuts with a miter saw.

The Delta Pro 3’s four AC plugs limit the number of appliances that can be plugged into it. We were forced to add a power strip to accommodate enough appliances to push its output limits. However, it does offer two different types of 220-volt outlets and a 30-amp RV outlet, along with four USB outlets for smaller devices. In addition to its power cable, this EcoFlow charges up with a car charger or via two solar ports for a total of 2,600 watts.

Referring to a large power station like this as “portable” is a bit of a stretch: The EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 weighs more than 113 pounds. Its two wheels and extendable handle allowed us to wheel it around a living room and kitchen like a piece of luggage, but it was difficult to move over a threshold between the garage and kitchen. The expansion pack sits on top of the power station, which saves space, but pushes the whole kit to a total weight of nearly 200 pounds.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easy-to-use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts, such as the Anker Solix C300 DC portable power station, typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models such as the EcoFlow Pro Delta 3, which can sustain a max output of up to 6,000 watts with a 4,000-watt-hour capacity, can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will backup critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn off and on inputs and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that it stays charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as an UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, thus can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or even the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#6451. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6449. Decades of clues helped scientists discover a massive freshwater lake miles beneath the ice in Antarctica

Lake Vostok, a vast freshwater lake hidden beneath 2.5 miles of Antarctic ice, was mapped using radar, seismic data and satellite measurements.

In June 1996, a paper in Nature described a large, deep freshwater lake beneath the ice of central East Antarctica. The lake, now called Lake Vostok, lies under about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) of ice.

The authors found that its area was about 50 percent larger than earlier estimates, with dimensions comparable to those of Lake Ontario.

The paper drew on clues that had been building for decades. They ranged from seismic soundings in the 1960s to airborne radar flights and, in 1993, satellite measurements.

The lake takes its name from Russia’s Vostok Station, which sits above its southern tip, according to Michael Studinger, then at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The former Soviet Union set up the station in 1957. It lies about 800 miles (1,300 kilometers) from the geographic South Pole, on roughly 2.3 miles (3,700 meters) of ice, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory.

About 30 people work at the station during the summer research season.

In 1983, the station’s air temperature fell to -129°F (-89°C).

Far below, the lake water sits under more than 360 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level.

Where the ice sheet crosses the lake, it goes afloat, Studinger writes. In some areas, lake water freezes onto the base of the ice.

Russian scientists suggested from seismic soundings in the 1960s that water might lie beneath the ice. Later, a joint U.S., British and Danish airborne radar project found flat reflections that pointed to water.

A 1974 to 1975 airborne radio-echo survey outlined a lake of about 3,900 square miles (10,000 square kilometers), the 1996 paper reports.

Robin Bell, a geophysicist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, described those flights in a NASA Earthdata feature.

“Scientists flew around Antarctica in C-130 airplanes that sent electromagnetic waves through the ice sheet,” Bell said.

The flat layers in the radar records were the first signs of subglacial lakes, or water trapped beneath the ice. At the time, researchers took them for small, isolated ponds.

“Quite frankly they didn’t seem to be important,” Bell recalled.

In the 1990s, the European Remote Sensing satellite, ERS-1, produced the first comprehensive map of Antarctica’s ice surface using radar altimetry, the same feature says.

Scientists studying that map noticed an unusually flat area near the center of the ice sheet, about the size of Lake Ontario.

“The ice surface will look rugged. But if water is underneath, the ice surface will look very flat,” Bell explained.

In 1993, satellite altimetry independently confirmed the extent of the lake first outlined by radar, the 1996 authors wrote.

The paper’s five authors came from Russian and British institutions. They included Andrey Kapitsa of Moscow State University and Martin Siegert, then at the University of Wales.

Another author was glaciologist Gordon de Quetteville Robin of the University of Cambridge’s Scott Polar Research Institute.

The team combined new altimetry and radio-echo data with existing seismic data. They found that the lake was deep, with an average depth of 410 feet (125 meters) or more, and that its water was fresh.

The team also estimated that water stays in the lake for tens of thousands of years. They put the mean age of the water at about one million years.

That age counts from when the water was deposited as surface ice on the ancient Antarctic ice sheet.

The regional flow of the ice could be explained as steady flow along and over the lake.

Robin had suggested in the 1950s that geothermal heat from the bedrock could warm the base of the ice sheet. He could not prove it until ice-penetrating radar arrived in the 1970s.

The base of the ice stays warm because of geothermal heating from Earth’s interior, Siegert wrote in a 2005 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences paper. About 50 milliwatts of heat per square meter is enough to melt the base of an ice sheet 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) thick.

The same review describes the lake as over 155 miles (250 kilometers) long, with depths reaching about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in places. It is one of over 100 subglacial lakes identified beneath Antarctica.

In 2012, a Russian team drilled all the way down to the lake to look for microbes, NASA’s Earth Observatory reported. Scientists estimate the lake has been sealed under ice for up to 25 million years.

Studinger also calls Lake Vostok the closest terrestrial analog to Europa, the ice-covered moon of Jupiter.

The study was published in the journal Nature.

#6448. The mystery of long COVID: What lasting health problems does the virus cause?

A massive study shows how comparison groups shape findings about long COVID and which lasting health problems are linked to the virus.

Long COVID can leave people feeling unwell long after an infection. But figuring out which health problems the virus caused depends partly on who researchers compare those patients with.

A Stanford University team found just how much that choice matters.

When the researchers repeated an approach used in earlier studies, it linked COVID to unlikely problems, including injuries from lightning, drowning, and electrocution.

Changing the comparison group produced a much shorter list of lasting effects. By the second year, none met the study’s cutoff, though that does not mean every patient had recovered.

The team drew on 14.4 billion insurance claims from nearly 245 million US patients.

These are bills from doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies, so they record medical care rather than how someone feels each day.

Between about four months and a year after infection, the revised approach linked 98% fewer health problems to COVID than the older method did using the same records.

Jure Leskovec, a Stanford computer science professor, was one of the study’s senior authors.

“This doesn’t mean long COVID is 98 percent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID,” Leskovec said.

Many earlier studies compared people who tested positive with people who had no recorded COVID diagnosis. That second group included people who tested negative and people who never took a test.

Those groups may differ before COVID enters the picture. Someone might get tested during a visit for diabetes or another illness, or because they see doctors more often.

“If you compare people who tested positive for COVID with people who were never tested, you risk attributing differences in their underlying health and healthcare-seeking behavior to the virus itself,” Leskovec said.

The concern is that researchers could end up blaming COVID for problems linked to someone’s existing health or reasons for seeking care.

The team compared people who tested negative and never had COVID recorded with untested people who had similar medical histories.

Between one and four months later, 82.5% of the health problems tracked were at least 10% more common in the group that tested negative.

A negative test could not explain those extra problems; the researchers pointed to other factors associated with getting tested.

For the main analysis, follow-up began with each patient’s first PCR test between March 1, 2020, and March 1, 2021.

The team compared positive results only with negative results, so everyone had a reason to get tested.

The researchers then adjusted the comparison group to match the positive group’s medical history over the previous four years.

They also matched age, sex, and neighborhood measures such as income.

This matching approach is called a synthetic control. Co-senior author Stefan Wager, an associate professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business, said economists commonly use it.

The records came from Komodo Health, which gathers claims from insurers, pharmacies, and programs including Medicare and Medicaid.

The researchers followed patients for up to two years and examined 614 health outcomes.

“Even with 244 million patients, you can get highly precise answers to the wrong question. Study design matters as much as data size,” Leskovec said.

As an initial check, the revised method picked up familiar COVID symptoms during the first month of infection.

Hamed Nilforoshan, a Stanford computer science doctoral student and one of three first authors, also recreated the older approach, closely following a 2021 Nature study. “Something wasn’t adding up,” Nilforoshan said.

The team checked 49 outcomes that COVID could not plausibly cause, including firearm injuries and birth defects recorded in adults. The older approach linked COVID to more than half.

It suggested a 76% increase in a category of injuries that included lightning, drowning, and electrocution. It also suggested an 18.6% increase in adults receiving diagnoses for birth defects of the eye, ear, face, or neck.

The authors said chance or flaws in study design presumably explained those unlikely links.

The revised approach flagged just two of the 49 outcomes, both showing lower risk after a positive test, which suggests it may slightly underestimate some real effects.

For the main results, a health problem had to increase by at least 10% and pass a strict statistical check that accounted for hundreds of comparisons.

From day 30 to day 119, the revised method linked 43 health problems to COVID, compared with 262 under the older method.

From about four months to a year, the revised method found five, compared with 286 under the older method. In the second year, those counts were zero and 369.

On average, recorded health problems in the positive group fell to roughly the comparison group’s level within a year. Earlier US veterans studies had found harmful effects after two or three years.

During the first months, COVID remained linked to problems involving the lungs, heart and blood vessels, kidneys, immune system, muscles, gut, and nervous system. Hair loss also appeared.

The biggest relative increase involved myopathy, a muscle disease, with related insurance claims about three times as common after a positive test.

Hair loss claims were nearly twice as common, while palpitations, malnutrition, and fatigue were 12% to 21% more common.

Between about four months and a year, five problems still met the cutoff: myopathy, hair loss, two categories of blood clots in the lungs, and respiratory failure.

Pneumonia, shortness of breath, chest pain, and fatigue increased by less than 10%. Even small increases in such common problems can affect many people.

Steven Goodman, a professor in Stanford Medicine’s Department of Epidemiology and Population Health, compared the findings with illnesses that linger after other infections.

“These findings indicate that long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought,” Goodman said.

Still, billing records can miss symptoms such as fatigue and brain fog.

The study also covered people who sought PCR testing through healthcare, leaving out infections identified only through home tests.

About 20% of the comparison group caught COVID within two years, which could make the virus’s effects look smaller. The study could not establish what caused symptoms that lasted beyond a year.

The authors stressed that lasting symptoms are real. Other illnesses that prompted the original test, or other factors, could help explain them, but these records cannot settle that question.

“These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them,” Leskovec said.

The team called for research into the biology of long COVID and biomarkers, measurable signs in the body that could help identify it.

They also suggested repeating earlier studies with comparison groups based on testing to see how much their results change.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6446. An old origami pattern inspires a new approach to construction

Researchers developed origami-inspired aluminum blocks that form lightweight, rigid structures, offering a potential new way to build emergency shelters.

Origami is usually something people do with paper. Using a folding pattern from the 1960s, researchers have turned flat sheets of aluminum into rigid building blocks.

Once they’re connected with ordinary hand tools, the blocks form a stiff, lightweight shell that holds itself up without any columns inside.

Every piece starts flat, so a whole structure could be shipped as a stack of panels and shaped by hand where it’s needed.

That makes the approach a candidate for relief shelters, set up quickly at the site of a natural disaster such as an earthquake or flood.

The method was developed by Alfonso Parra Rubio, a graduate student at the MIT Center for Bits and Atoms, with colleagues in Italy, Austria, and Japan. The center studies how to turn digital designs into physical things.

So far, the team’s strength figures come from computer simulations, and the approach hasn’t yet been tried on a full-size building.

“This work shows that the power of digital manufacturing can go beyond personal fabrication projects and start touching the real world, enhancing the way we design houses and large structures,” said Parra Rubio, the paper’s lead author.

“We are demonstrating structural origami on building scales.”

Parra Rubio’s design builds on the folded patterns that the artist and scientist Ron Resch developed in the 1960s.

Resch repeated small many-sided cells across a surface to build complex 3D shapes, and each shape came from a single folded sheet.

The new method folds each small unit on its own and connects the units afterward. Building from separate blocks makes the parts simpler to produce, and it lets the team create more complicated shapes.

Working in the lab of Tomohiro Tachi at the University of Tokyo, Parra Rubio found a way to pair two tripod-shaped units from a Resch pattern into one block.

Pairing the units locks their folds in place, creating a rigid block.

Joined together, the blocks form a hexagonal grid of interwoven beams. The grid is extremely stiff and stable, yet it weighs very little.

“This helps us build strong structures while minimizing the amount of material we are using,” Parra Rubio said.

Designing every block by hand, so that the finished structure matches the shape a builder wants, would be enormously difficult.

Parra Rubio teamed up with Erik Strand, another graduate student at the center, to write a program that does the job automatically.

The program designs a set of blocks that can be cut, folded, and joined to form the requested shape.

The resulting surface can curve in one direction or in two directions, as a dome does.

From there, the design files are sent to a computer-controlled milling machine, which cuts the blocks out of flat sheets of material such as aluminum.

“On the computational part, we break this big problem down into many small subproblems. Now, we solve each cell independently to make sure that it is foldable, and then we globally assemble them after that,” Strand said.

Builders fold each unit into shape and put the structure together with hand tools such as screwdrivers.

Assembly requires no welding equipment, which could make construction simpler, faster, and cheaper.

The units are also designed so that each one takes its correct shape as the structure goes together.

“The way the unit cells are designed, the structure can only exist in one configuration. The connection is the same everywhere, even though each unit cell is different,” Parra Rubio said.

In the team’s computer simulations, shells built this way came out about 3.5 times stiffer than those made with some other origami-based methods. They also needed only about two-thirds as much material.

Because the method could reduce metal use, it may be a more sustainable form of construction.

Parra Rubio said the finished structures could be strong enough for some architectural uses.

The method could also produce strong, lightweight parts for airplanes and for modular robots, along with panels that dampen sound and the outer walls of buildings.

To show that the method works beyond small prototypes, the team assembled a 23-foot (7-meter) sculpture from folded aluminum.

It was hung from the ceiling of the atrium at the Boston Public Library, as part of an exhibition opened for the annual Fab Lab Conference and Symposium.

A team with no professional construction experience built the entire sculpture in a matter of days, Parra Rubio said.

“It was really fun to work on something at such a quick pace where the theory was really meeting a practical use for it. We had to think a lot about how we could tweak the design to achieve each objective,” Strand said.

The researchers next plan to test the approach on larger architectural structures.

The team also wants to try units with more complex shapes, which might offer more strength or stiffness. And they hope to build a design program that’s easy to use.

Neil Gershenfeld, an MIT professor who directs the center, was the paper’s senior author.

“This work shows that folding metal is a method that is ready to be used for building structures,” Gershenfeld said.

“We can do it big enough and strong enough, now that we can bring it out of the lab and to the construction site.”

Larger tests will show whether folded aluminum performs as well in a real building as it did in the simulations.

The full study was published in the journal International Journal of Solids and Structures.

#6445. A virtual escape may help children feel less scared before surgery

Children reported less fear after brief virtual reality sessions before surgery, offering early evidence for a possible drug-free calming option.

Before an operation, plenty of children are scared, and a common way to calm them is a sedative that carries risks of its own.

Researchers tested a drug-free option: a virtual reality headset showing a calm playroom or a quiet beach.

After a short session in it, children said they felt less upset and less scared, while their heart rates went down.

Whether the headset deserves the credit is still an open question.

Walaa Abu Rukbah, a pharmacist at the University of Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, is the study’s first author.

“Sometimes, the best support we can offer a child before surgery isn’t a medicine at all,” said Abu Rukbah.

The project ran for nine months at a children’s hospital in Virginia. Every child in it used the headset, so there was no group of children who waited without one to compare against.

Between half and three-quarters of children feel anxious before surgery, by the researchers’ estimate.

A scared child isn’t only unhappy. Very anxious children are more likely to struggle when it’s time to go under anesthesia.

They’re also more likely to wake up confused and agitated, a state doctors call emergence delirium, and to have more pain and a slower recovery.

The calming drug used most often is midazolam. It can make some children more agitated instead of calmer, and it can slow breathing or delay the trip home.

Drug-free options such as play therapy and music have helped children in earlier studies, but they need trained staff that not every hospital has.

The team spent 10 months designing its own virtual world for children.

The main scene is a playroom in soft blues and greens, with toys that respond when a child looks at them and slow music in the background.

A second scene shows a beach with waves and palm trees.

Some people experience motion sickness in virtual reality because what they see does not match the motion their body senses.

To avoid that, children hop from spot to spot instead of gliding around. When 15 children tried it early on, none of them reported feeling sick.

From October 2023 to June 2024, 80 children aged 6 to 15 used the headset while waiting for planned surgery at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU.

Their parents could watch on a tablet what the child was seeing. A typical session lasted about nine minutes, though some ran as long as 20.

Before and after each session, children rated how upset they felt from 0 to 10, much like the pain scales doctors use.

They also pointed to one of five faces, ranging from calm to very scared.

The typical child’s score dropped from 3 to 1 on the 0-to-10 scale. On the faces, the typical child pointed to the second face before the session and the calmest face after it.

Not every child changed much. By the team’s measure of a change big enough to matter, 46 of the 80 children felt noticeably less upset afterward and 44 felt noticeably less scared. That’s a little more than half.

Bedside monitors picked up a change too. Heart rate dropped by nearly six beats a minute on average.

Systolic blood pressure – the top number in a blood pressure reading – fell by about 4 points on average.

Only three children had any side effects, and all of them were minor.

Dayanjan Wijesinghe, a researcher in the Department of Pharmacotherapy and Outcomes Science at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), was also involved in the study.

“In a busy children’s surgical unit, a short virtual reality session proved easy for nurses to run, was safe, and was very popular: nine in ten children wanted to use it again, and nearly every parent would recommend it,” said Wijesinghe.

All 29 nurses involved said they would recommend it too.

When parents wrote about the experience, they mentioned distraction more than anything else.

“He was distracted and didn’t notice when the needle went in,” one parent wrote.

Not every parent was equally enthusiastic.

“If my child chose it, sure. To me it’s a bit overwhelming to have so much going on,” another parent wrote.

Waiting rooms can get easier on their own. A child might calm down simply from getting used to the room, or from having an adult pay close attention for a while.

The most scared children had the biggest drops.

However, unusually high initial scores can fall on a second measurement even without an effective treatment, potentially making the headset appear more helpful.

Scientists call this regression to the mean, and it can make health programs look better than they really are.

The team’s own checks suggested it explains much of why the most anxious children improved the most.

Families also knew they were trying something new, and the study team collected their ratings in person. That can lead people to give kinder answers.

Once the children left the waiting room, the researchers stopped tracking them.

Whether a calmer wait leads to an easier start to anesthesia or a faster recovery wasn’t measured.

All of the children came from a single hospital, so a hospital with different staff or patients might see different results.

In the researchers’ view, the next step is a randomized trial that compares the headset with usual care and with other drug-free options.

Such a trial could also show whether a headset costs less than giving children a sedative.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Digital Health.

#6444. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

#6441. California schools must drop ultra-processed food, and kitchen managers explain why that’s hard

California will phase ultra-processed foods out of school meals, but kitchen directors say money, staff and small kitchens stand in the way.

Taking junk food off school menus sounds like a matter of writing a rule. California has written one, and starting in 2029 its schools must begin phasing out many ultra-processed foods.

But when researchers asked the people who run school kitchens what makes cooking from scratch hard, the answers were money, staff and kitchens built mostly to reheat.

Many districts even buy basic ingredients, then pay to have them turned into the processed foods that the law targets.

That’s the gap between a law and a lunch line, and the directors said closing it will take more than a deadline.

The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act requires California schools to begin phasing out certain ultra-processed foods in July 2029 and finish by 2035. These are factory-made foods with ingredients that home cooks rarely use, such as flavorings, colorings and emulsifiers.

Such foods make up about two-thirds of the calories U.S. children eat, according to studies the authors cite. School meals can supply about half of a child’s daily calories, which makes the cafeteria a big lever on what kids eat.

Andrea Pedroza-Tobias, then an instructor at Stanford Medicine and now at UC Irvine, led the study with pediatrician Anisha Patel.

Community groups, including the Dolores Huerta Foundation and Cultiva La Salud, helped shape it, along with the Nutrition Policy Institute at the University of California.

From January to June 2024, the team interviewed food service directors from 20 school districts in California’s San Joaquin Valley, a farming region with many low-income families.

The districts were picked at random from urban and rural areas, and from districts with and without a state grant for freshly prepared meals.

Sixteen of the directors also filled out a short survey. On average, their districts served some scratch-cooked items about 2.5 days a week and heat-and-serve foods about 3 days a week.

That is a small group in one region. The authors note that the results may not match other parts of the country, and that directors who agreed to talk may care more about scratch cooking than those who didn’t.

Two-thirds of the surveyed directors identified staff shortages and a lack of money for labor as obstacles. Many rely on part-time workers who can reheat food but don’t have time to cook it. Storage and kitchen space came next.

State grants for kitchen equipment helped, but the money went different ways. Some districts bought skillets and ranges for cooking, while others bought more ovens to assist with reheating. Directors also said one-year grants made it hard to plan for the long run.

Most did credit California’s free meals for every student with bringing in more money, and in some districts more cooks.

In an interview with Earth.com, Patel and Pedroza-Tobias said the money has to come with guidelines for using it. “However, funding alone is not enough,” they said. They pointed to policies, practices and technical assistance paired with funding.

Schools get raw ingredients through a federal food program, but many districts ship them out to be processed. “I’m sending my chicken to, let’s say, Tyson and getting chicken patties and chicken nuggets,” one director told the researchers.

Directors also said most products labeled and sold for schools, the ones built to meet federal nutrition rules, are ultra-processed.

Amanda Harvey, who runs nutrition services for Fresno Unified and sat on the study’s advisory board, has seen supply problems firsthand. When her district dropped products with food dye, pickles made without green dye became hard to find.

“They’re pricey for pickles, and it can be quite challenging for our vendor to get them,” Harvey said. Another director recalled spending years removing cooking equipment and buying more processed food, and now using grant money to buy the same kinds of kettles and skillets back.

Some directors worried students would skip scratch-cooked meals and throw more food away. Others said students preferred fresh, familiar food, and they described ways to win kids over, including taste tests, family nutrition nights and student recipe contests.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised them most, the researchers pointed to districts that found creative ways around tight budgets. “One food service director even dressed in costumes to encourage children to try healthier foods,” they said.

They also noted that at least seven other states have passed laws on specific food additives or dyes, though most still allow some ultra-processed foods. Brazil’s national school meal program, they said, requires at least 85 percent of federal food funds to go to fresh or minimally processed foods.

The directors described what they expect and what they’ve tried. The study didn’t measure what children actually ate, how their health changed, or whether the new law’s timeline is realistic.

The authors call for money to hire and keep staff, upgrade kitchens and train cooks, along with rules that make ultra-processed products less attractive to buy.

Whether California’s districts can make that switch by 2035 will show up on real trays over the next decade, and no one has measured it yet.

Research on kids’ behavior and toddler foods has kept attention on processed food in childhood, and on its health risks. Schools may be where the change is easiest to track.

The full study was published in the journal Public Health Nutrition.

#6440. The 9 Best Ductless Air Conditioners for Efficient Home Cooling

Whether you want a budget-friendly option or a high-efficiency heat pump for year-round comfort, these are the best ductless air conditioners to consider right now.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

To help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

For this update, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners.
