#6431. The 6 Best Smart Thermostats to Keep Your House Comfortable and Save You Money

Get more efficient heating and cooling with these set-it-and-forget-it models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

For the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

It doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

The ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

The smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t currently in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

For a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

Honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”

With a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

While the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That said, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

Another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

If this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

They’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. Here at Popular Mechanics, Tom loves testing out home appliances, smart tech, gear for city life and outdoor adventures, small gadgets like watches and multitools, and anything else you can find piled up at his hoarder's nest of a desk.

Prior to working here, Tom attended NYU, graduating with a degree in English and a minor in creative writing. He also wrote for Best Reviews, The Daily Beast, and other publications covering tech, fitness gear, gadgets, and lifestyle products. #6430. Giant crane bones reveal a surprising case of mistaken identity

Ancient DNA suggests a giant crane thought extinct for 150 years was a common crane, a bird still living in Europe that used to be bigger.

For more than 150 years, unusually large crane bones found across Europe were often credited to an extinct giant called Grus primigenia.

Ancient DNA from a sample of those bones now points to the common crane, a bird that still lives in Europe and used to grow bigger than it does today.

So the giant may never have been a species of its own.

John Stewart, a professor of evolutionary paleoecology at Bournemouth University in England, led the work.

His team read DNA from 18 crane bones found in England, Wales, France, Germany and Spain’s Balearic Islands.

The original bone used to describe the proposed species wasn’t tested.

Alphonse Milne-Edwards, a French biologist, described the crane in the 19th century.

His key specimen was the lower end of a leg bone from a cave at Les Eyzies, in southern France. It was wider from side to side than the same bone in a sarus crane, a large crane from Asia.

Experts argued about the bones for more than a century. Some accepted the giant as a real, extinct bird.

Others thought the bones belonged to sarus cranes or Siberian white cranes, both still living in Asia, or to extra-large common cranes.

Among the extinct prehistoric birds of Europe and northern Asia, only the great auk has drawn more debate, the authors wrote.

“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart said.

The DNA work was done at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden. Researchers drilled about 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) of powder from each bone.

They analyzed mitochondrial DNA, which is passed down from mothers, and compared it with sequences from living cranes.

All 18 bones matched the common crane, oversized ones included. The sarus crane and the Siberian white crane turned out to be distant relatives, which ruled both of them out.

Some researchers had wondered whether Britain once had its own large type of common crane, but the samples gave no sign of such a crane.

The British birds’ DNA was mixed in with that of birds from mainland Europe, and the team has posted the raw data in the European Nucleotide Archive, a public database.

“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes,” Stewart said.

“We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species – the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species.”

In birds, males carry two copies of a sex chromosome called Z, while females carry one Z and one W.

Relative to DNA from other chromosomes, females have about half as much Z chromosome DNA as males.

The team used this difference to identify the sex of most specimens. Nearly every bone from a male was as big as a modern male’s or bigger.

The female bones mostly fell between today’s female and male sizes, and none had measurements that matched only modern females. Female cranes in the past were larger, too.

One thigh bone was found at Le Morin, a rock shelter in southwestern France.

In both measurements the team could take, it exceeded the modern common crane bones used for comparison. DNA analysis showed that it belonged to a female.

Earlier work on the bone found cut marks and a type of tissue suggesting people butchered her in the breeding season.

The youngest large cranes the team knows of come from Flixborough, an Anglo-Saxon settlement in northern England.

People lived there from the late 600s to the early 1000s, and excavations uncovered 229 crane remains.

Common cranes got smaller after that, within roughly the last thousand years.

That timing is unusual: size changes in other animals more often date to the end of the last ice age.

The mute swan also appears to have shrunk over the past 11,700 years, the authors noted.

A 2023 study estimated that roughly 1,300 to 1,500 bird species have been lost since the late ice age.

By that estimate, more than half of those bird extinctions haven’t been discovered. Stewart’s team wrote that such claims need careful studies of single species like this one.

Many extinct birds from Europe and northern Asia were named mostly from size and shape, and confirming them may take the same kind of ancient DNA work.

“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past. Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he said.

Milne-Edwards’ original bone, kept at the Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle in Paris, wasn’t sampled because testing would damage it.

The French cave bones in the study come from the same late ice age period, about 15,000 to 17,500 years ago. So the authors expect the Paris bone to be a common crane too, though a small doubt remains until it’s tested.

A bigger open question is why the cranes shrank.

The authors listed climate change, wetland drainage and other changes in how people use land as possible causes, but called each one speculation for now.

“The challenge going forwards is to investigate the reason for the cranes’ decrease in size,” Stewart said.

“Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that.”

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6429. America shines before sunrise in a stunning astronaut photo

An astronaut’s predawn photo captures Midwest cities shining beneath colorful airglow, revealing what nighttime lights can tell us about Earth.

In the darkness before dawn, city lights sketch a glowing map of the American Midwest.

Cities shine across the dark landscape, and a faint glow traces the atmosphere above them.

Today’s Image of the Day captures this meeting of electric light and natural light from the International Space Station.

An astronaut took the wide-angle photograph on October 18, 2026, at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time, or 09:54 Universal Time.

With clear skies across much of the eastern United States, the camera recorded an expansive view of communities still waiting for dawn.

Chicago and Detroit form two of the scene’s brightest concentrations.

Between and beyond these major metropolitan areas, smaller clusters mark cities including Indianapolis, Cincinnati, and Louisville.

Illuminated routes help connect those bright centers, showing how settlements extend across the region.

From orbit, these corridors reveal connections among cities that can be difficult to appreciate from the ground.

The broad perspective also changes how individual cities look.

Chicago appears as a largely uniform patch of pale yellow in this photograph, although closer views reveal differences in the colors of its lighting.

Those variations matter. Different kinds of lamps give off different mixtures of light, leaving clues that researchers can examine in detailed astronaut photographs.

Above the cities, the photograph records light with a very different origin.

Along the left side of the horizon, green and orange bands mark airglow, a faint radiance produced by gases in Earth’s upper atmosphere.

Solar energy sets the process in motion, and atoms and molecules release light as they shed energy.

Airglow can persist through the night. Although its colors may resemble an aurora, the two phenomena have different drivers: auroras arise from energetic particles, while airglow draws its energy from ordinary solar radiation.

On the right, sunlight brightens the horizon as morning approaches.

At the time of the photograph, sunrise was still roughly an hour away along the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago.

Daylight photographs show the Midwest through its fields, waterways, and buildings.

At night, artificial lighting draws attention to a different set of features: where people have built communities and how those places connect.

Large cities dominate the view, but the smaller patches of light help fill in the picture.

Together, they show a region made up of many distinct communities, with illuminated corridors stretching between them.

Dark areas require more careful interpretation. A place without obvious lights is not necessarily empty.

Land used for farming, for example, can support substantial human activity while producing relatively little nighttime illumination.

The photograph shows where light reaches the camera, rather than providing a complete inventory of what lies below.

Scale also shapes what viewers can learn. This wide view makes regional patterns easier to recognize, while detailed photographs allow researchers to investigate differences within a single city.

Moving between those perspectives helps turn a beautiful scene into useful information.

The broad image shows how the pieces fit together; closer observations reveal details that disappear when an entire metropolitan area becomes one bright patch against the night.

Views like this offer more than a striking portrait of Earth after dark. Repeated observations help scientists examine how human settlements change over time.

Researchers using NASA’s Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive have developed a method for identifying lighting types within nighttime images.

Measuring the color, brightness, and spread of urban illumination can help document changes in the built environment.

Satellite observations add another way to follow those changes.

NASA’s Black Marble products provide records of nighttime lighting at daily, monthly, and yearly intervals.

Scientists have used these observations to track power losses and the return of electricity after major storms.

This photograph preserves a quieter moment: cities glowing beneath an atmosphere that produces light of its own.

Soon, daylight would make both harder to see, concealing the luminous patterns that briefly bring the region into focus.

Image Credit: ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, NASA Johnson Space Center

#6428. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6427. A wrist sensor worn at home tracked stroke recovery more precisely than clinic tests

A wrist sensor worn for a day at home scored stroke recovery with about half the measurement error of clinic tests, and could shrink trials.

After a stroke, the usual way to track recovery is a therapist watching you work through a set of tasks for half an hour. Most patients get that test before rehab and again when it ends.

However, these two scores, months apart, can’t tell a therapist whether a patient is responding in week three.

Researchers have now turned a day of readings from a wrist sensor worn at home into a stroke recovery score. It tracked the same changes with about half the measurement error of those clinic tests.

A clinical trial built on the score could also reach a reliable answer with more than 60 percent fewer patients, the team calculated.

Sunghoon Ivan Lee of the Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst led the work with his graduate student Ryan Wang. Colleagues at WashU Medicine, Shirley Ryan AbilityLab and Spaulding Rehabilitation joined them.

The team didn’t build a new gadget. They reanalyzed about 23,000 hours of wrist recordings already collected from 215 people, and wrote the software that turns those recordings into a score.

Researchers call a measure like that a digital biomarker.

In an interview with Earth.com, Lee said the size of the gain surprised him. “We found that our digital biomarker is almost twice as precise as current clinical standard assessments,” he said.

In the two standard tests, the therapist scores each task on a fixed scale. Each takes about 30 minutes and a trained specialist to run, so in practice it happens before therapy and after it.

Both tests also have a ceiling. A patient at the maximum score has, by that measure, nothing left to recover, even when the arm still doesn’t work the way it did.

“That means during that therapy process, neither the patient nor the therapist has a clear idea of how patients are responding to the treatments that they’re receiving,” Lee said.

The recordings came from three earlier studies in St. Louis. One followed 61 people through standard rehab in the first six months of stroke recovery. They came back for up to eight clinic visits over 24 weeks.

Those were the patients whose arms were changing fastest. Another followed 79 people at least six months past a stroke, through an eight-week arm therapy trial. The third enrolled 75 healthy adults.

After each clinic visit, everyone wore a small motion sensor, the kind inside fitness trackers, on each wrist for about a day at home.

The software reads only the stroke-affected wrist. It picks out the straight-line movements that make up most daily tasks, such as reaching for an object, and measures how fast, how abruptly and how variously the arm moved.

A model then combines those measurements into one number, matched to the clinic score, on a scale with no ceiling.

In the early-stage group, the score agreed closely with both clinic tests. Over 24 weeks, its average rose along almost the same curve as the therapists’ scores.

Its measurement error was 52 to 58 percent lower than that of the clinic tests, which is where Lee’s “almost twice as precise” comes from.

Then there were the patients who had hit the top of a clinic test. Their wrist scores were still lower than the healthy adults’ scores, a gap that the clinic scales can’t show because they have no room above the top mark.

Asked by Earth.com what else the data showed, Lee named that gap. “We discovered that our digital biomarker can differentiate stroke survivors who received a perfect clinical score from healthy subjects,” he said.

“This is significant because it shows the biomarker detects subtle motor performance differences that current clinical standards cannot.”

A less noisy measure means a clinical trial needs fewer people to show that a treatment works. The team reran two past trials in simulation, with the score standing in for the clinic test.

In a trial of robot-assisted therapy, an 80 percent chance of confirming the treatment effect took eight patients per group with the clinic test, and three with the score.

In a second trial, the number fell from 26 per group to seven. These are simulations built on statistical assumptions, the authors wrote, not real trial results.

“We can get a clear idea of the effectiveness of the intervention using a lower sample size and far fewer resources,” Lee said.

The long-term group is where the score’s limits show. Those patients barely changed over eight weeks of therapy on either measure, so the data can’t say whether the score picks up improvement years after a stroke.

The healthy adults were a little younger than the stroke survivors, and they were never tested in the clinic; the team assigned them perfect scores.

Each person wore the sensor for one day per visit, so the reliability figures come from splitting that day in half rather than from two separate days.

And the sensor records acceleration alone, which forces the software to estimate gravity’s share of the signal. The team wants a gyroscope added in future versions.

Lee has filed a provisional patent and is pursuing the technology through a startup, Lumid Health, so he stands to gain if it reaches patients.

“The hardware is already there; accelerometer sensors are standard in modern fitness trackers and smartwatches,” Lee told Earth.com.

“However, translation into clinical practice requires rigorous third-party validation on independent datasets and regulatory approval, which could take years.”

What the score would give a stroke survivor, he said, is a day-by-day read on whether the prescribed exercises are working.

The study measured how well the score tracks recovery. It did not test whether a therapist who sees that number every day treats a patient differently, or whether the patient ends up better off.

Lee’s partners are recruiting stroke survivors for a follow-up study at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital. Other groups will have to confirm the score on recordings this team never touched.

The full study was published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

#6425. Archaeologists Found 120,000-Year-Old Human Footprints Where They Shouldn’t Be

They might just rewrite the story of human migration—as a tale of who failed, not who survived.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between roughly 112,000 and 121,000 years ago, a handful of people walked along the muddy shore of a lake in what is now Saudi Arabia’s Nefud Desert. Elephants and camels had churned up the ground, and the humans left seven footprints among hundreds of animal tracks before sediment sealed the whole scene for eternity. When researchers described the site, called Alathar (Arabic for “the trace”), in a 2020 paper in Science Advances, we called the prints “the oldest-ever human footprints on the Arabian Peninsula” and marveled that they had survived at all. As the researchers noted, an experimental study of modern footprints in mud flats “found that fine details were lost within two days and prints were rendered unrecognizable within four.”

Six years later, the original interpretation still holds. “The age estimate remains about 120,000 years ago based on scientific dating,” Michael Petraglia, an archaeologist at Griffith University in Australia who studies human evolution and dispersal, tells Popular Mechanics. “The size and shape of the footprints are consistent with Homo sapiens.” What has changed is the record around them. Petraglia says sites dated since 2020 suggest that people entered Arabia when wetter weather filled the peninsula with lakes. During these “Green Arabia” periods, people could find drinking water in places that are now desert. When the water disappeared, some of those populations may have disappeared with it, possibly including the people who left the Alathar tracks.

Arabia went through this cycle many times. For a 2021 study in Nature, Huw Groucutt, Petraglia, and their colleagues dated ancient lake deposits in the Nefud that contained stone tools and animal fossils. They found that human ancestors moved into the Arabian interior at least five times between about 400,000 and 55,000 years ago, each time during a wetter spell, and each phase had its own style of stone tools. “This looks like different populations, and indeed species, moving into the area at different times,” says Groucutt, an archaeologist and senior lecturer at the University of Malta who studies human prehistory and environmental change. Once the rains stopped, he says, there probably wasn’t enough water for anyone to stay.

Even in the good years, people probably kept moving. Groucutt pictures groups traveling among scattered small lakes and other water sources in a landscape that was still highly seasonal, with very hot summers. Alathar fits that picture. The researchers found no stone tools or butchered bones at the site and concluded that the lake “was only briefly visited by people,” most likely for drinking water. For Petraglia, that brevity is what makes the tracks valuable. “Footprints capture a moment in time, illustrating that people walked along lakeshores at the same time as animals,” he says.

These walkers may have no living descendants

If the Alathar walkers were Homo sapiens, Groucutt thinks they belonged to a branch of humanity that didn’t make it. “The dominant view from genetics is that people living outside Africa today descend from people spreading into Asia around 50 to 80,000 years ago, so earlier people died out,” he says. By that reasoning, the footprints are “probably an example of an earlier, failed, migration.” That kind of failed migration is also known from other sites, including Skhul Cave on Mount Carmel, where fossils of early Homo sapiens were found. Reaching Arabia, then, came with no guarantee of surviving there. The people who left these tracks may have died out, and a much later migration brought the ancestors of most people living outside Africa today. Petraglia describes the same pattern of shifting fortunes: “Migrations were repeated movements, with groups expanding, contracting, and possibly disappearing from parts of the peninsula as conditions changed.”

As Arabia dried, Groucutt thinks, people may have retreated south, following the water into the wetter parts of the peninsula. Differences in stone tools suggest that these southern populations developed their own ways of doing things as they lost contact with people farther north. But the south eventually dried up too. Groucutt reads gaps in the archaeological record as a sign that the remaining groups became too small and isolated to make it through the worst dry spells. The same lakes that drew people into Arabia could leave them stranded, crowded around whatever water remained and with fewer and fewer places to go. The Alathar tracks date to a dry spell during the last interglacial, which puts their makers in exactly this kind of shrinking landscape.

The proof is hard to find in a hot desert

Settling the question will take evidence that a desert doesn’t give up easily. Groucutt would welcome hominin fossils, though he doubts they would be the “smoking gun” people sometimes imagine, since bones can be hard to date and hard to assign to a species. Ancient DNA could do more, but in low latitudes it “just doesn’t go that far back,” he says, because “hot places are bad for preservation.” Petraglia is hunting for something more specific. “A securely dated human fossil or a long, stratified sequence showing human occupations across both wet and dry periods would be transformative,” he says. Working with Saudi colleagues who help choose sites and reach them, his team is searching around former water sources for evidence of people who stayed as the climate changed.

Until that evidence turns up, the Alathar footprints remain one of the few direct records of these early travelers. If they left no descendants, the site’s name may best describe what survives of them: a trace.

#6424. What came before land plants? New genetic clues reveal a complicated story

A new genetic study traces the complex history of land plants’ closest algal relatives, revealing repeated shifts from single cells to filaments.

Every tree, flower, and blade of grass on Earth belongs to a lineage that evolved from freshwater algae roughly 500 million years ago.

Reconstructing what those ancient ancestors looked like means looking closely at their living relatives.

New genetic evidence suggests that the common ancestor of land plants’ closest living algal relatives was a single cell.

Within that algal group, filamentous growth evolved independently at least seven times. The findings reveal a branching history in which multicellular forms arose repeatedly.

The study was led by researchers at the University of Göttingen.

The group in question is the Zygnematophyceae. This is a class of freshwater algae whose simple appearance once made them seem unlikely candidates for land plants’ closest living algal relatives.

Some are just single cells. Others form filaments.

The most famous is Spirogyra, that green slime recognizable by its spiral chloroplasts winding through each cell.

For years, more complex-looking algae like Chara and Coleochaete seemed like better candidates for land plant ancestors. Genomics flipped that assumption on its head.

Maaike Bierenbroodspot conducted the research during her PhD at Göttingen and is now a postdoc at the University of Maastricht.

“Many zygnematophytes look deceptively simple, but their genomes reveal a remarkably deep and complex evolutionary history and diversity,” said Bierenbroodspot.

“We can begin to see evolutionary events that remain invisible when we study only a handful of model species.”

Previous phylogenomic work on zygnematophytes had relied on just a handful of genomes. To fill the gaps, the team generated 43 new transcriptomes.

These capture RNA produced by genes active under the sampled conditions.

Combined with existing data, the final dataset covered 104 species and 2,243 genetic loci.

The resulting family tree divides the Zygnematophyceae into five orders: Desmidiales, Spirogloeales, Zygnematales, Spirogyrales, and Serritaeniales.

One of the most striking features is the branch leading to modern Spirogyra species. It is 6.2 times longer than the branch to its sister group, the Desmidiales.

That extreme genetic distance hints at either massive extinction within Spirogyrales, vast unsampled diversity still lurking in freshwater habitats, or dramatically accelerated rates of molecular evolution.

The team then used the family tree to reconstruct the likely appearance of the common ancestor of all zygnematophytes.

The analysis strongly favored a single-celled ancestor.

Filamentous growth then evolved independently multiple times across the tree. The researchers count at least seven separate transitions from single-celled to filamentous body plans.

That number gets even more interesting when you consider that not all filaments are built the same way.

Spirogyra and Zygnema form what biologists call bona fide filaments – cells dividing and staying connected in true multicellular threads.

But desmids, which are typically unicellular, sometimes form “chain-like filaments.” These are individual cells that simply remain stuck together end-to-end after dividing.

The distinction matters. These are fundamentally different solutions to the problem of becoming bigger than a single cell.

The genomes also revealed something profound about how land plants assembled their molecular toolkit.

Genes once thought to be exclusively plant inventions turn up scattered across the zygnematophyte tree.

This happened in a patchy, lineage-specific pattern telling a story of dynamic gain and loss rather than steady accumulation.

“These algae have genes that are part of what we call the ‘land plant heritage,’” said Cäcilia Kunz from the University of Göttingen.

“They show that some of the molecular components associated with important plant functions have much deeper evolutionary histories than the land plants themselves.”

“At the same time, their distribution across algal lineages shows that this evolutionary toolkit was dynamic.”

Take the PYR/PYL/RCAR genes, which in land plants encode receptors for abscisic acid – the stress hormone that helps plants survive drought.

These genes show up in Mesotaenium and Zygnema but are absent from desmids like Penium and Closterium.

That suggests they were present in the common ancestor but lost in certain lineages.

Or consider CAD – cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase – a key enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway that ultimately produces lignin, the molecule that makes wood hard.

CAD homologs turned up across the zygnematophyte tree. Yet, none fell into the classes typically found in land plants.

Instead, they formed their own distinct groupings, with protein structure predictions suggesting they function more like sinapyl alcohol dehydrogenases.

The findings suggest that related enzymes existed before land plants, although their functions may have differed.

The histidine kinases tell a similar story. These ancient signaling proteins, which in land plants help perceive light and the hormone cytokinin, have undergone massive expansion in zygnematophytes.

PAS-domain-containing histidine kinases – involved in light sensing – turned out to be particularly abundant and diverse.

The study represents the most comprehensive phylogenomic framework for zygnematophytes to date, but the authors are the first to acknowledge its limits.

The dataset covers 104 species out of more than 4,000 described, leaving much of the group’s diversity unexplored.

Within Zygnema alone, molecular clock analysis places the divergence between two species at 236 million years ago, underscoring just how ancient these lineages are.

“Our study gives us a much better map of the evolutionary landscape surrounding the origin of land plants,” said Jan de Vries from the University of Göttingen.

“The more diversity we include, the more we see that evolution was not a simple progression from single-celled algae to increasingly complex plants.”

“Instead, different lineages experimented with different body plans and molecular solutions over hundreds of millions of years.”

“Understanding this diversity is crucial if we want to reconstruct the biology of the algal ancestors from which land plants emerged.”

The study is published in the journal PLOS Biology.

#6423. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6422. A forgotten 1967 LSD pamphlet warned first-timers what could go wrong, and today’s users mostly agree

Lisa Bieberman's 1967 LSD pamphlet urged trust, patience and no mirrors. A survey of 496 experienced users backed 18 of her 19 tips.

The 1960s LSD scene is mostly remembered through Timothy Leary, the Harvard psychology lecturer who urged a generation to “turn on, tune in, and drop out.”

One of his former followers spent those same years on a less famous question: what goes wrong on a trip, and how to stop it.

More than half a century later, experienced psychedelic users still agree with nearly all of the advice she gave beginners. Advice that history largely forgot has, by this measure, aged well.

Daniel Kruger, a research associate professor at the University at Buffalo, surveyed today’s users with Paul Gillis-Smith of Harvard Divinity School’s Center for the Study of World Religions.

Co-authors came from the Michigan Psychedelic Center at the University of Michigan and from community groups in Ann Arbor and Southfield.

The team asked people whether they agreed with the advice, not whether following it had kept anyone safe.

Lisa Bieberman studied at Radcliffe College, then the women’s sister college to Harvard. After graduating in 1963 she went to work for a group that Leary and Richard Alpert had founded.

In 1965, she started what she called a Psychedelic Information Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She published regular, nationwide newsletters on LSD use.

The problem on the scene, she wrote, was “one of widespread misinformation and not knowing who to believe,” and her publications were part of her effort to counter this.

In 1967 Bieberman published a book titled Session Games People Play: A Manual for the Use of LSD. It cost $1 by mail and covered drug laws, gatherings and practical tips on the use of psychedelics, especially for first-timers.

“This book then is no tourist’s guide through paradise, but a down-to-earth discussion of the sorts of things that can go wrong in an LSD session and how to prevent them,” she wrote. The first thousand copies sold out quickly.

Her “games” were habits to avoid during a trip, like running away from your companions, or deciding you’ve unlocked the deepest truths of the universe and need to tell the world.

The team turned 19 pieces of her advice into survey statements. Ten covered getting ready, and nine covered the session itself. People rated each one on a scale running from strongly disagree to strongly agree.

Recruiting ran online and at Entheofest, a psychedelic advocacy event in Ann Arbor, Michigan, in September and October 2023.

The analysis covered 496 adults who had taken a full dose of a psychedelic, and left out people who had only microdosed.

Nearly all of them had used psilocybin mushrooms in the past, about half had taken LSD, and most had used a psychedelic within the past year. And 58.5 percent held a role that called for psychedelic expertise, such as guide or sitter, therapist, or educator.

On average, participants agreed with 18 of the 19 statements. For getting ready, the strongest support went to “Be with people who all know, like, and trust each other,” and to “Be aware that even with a guide, you have to do most of the work yourself.”

During the session, two statements did best. One was “Recognize that the experience will eventually end.” The other was “Recognize that you may experience anxiety, which does not mean that something is wrong.”

On the first point, Bieberman had been blunter. Asking friends to bring you down, she wrote, “is as practical as asking your fellow passengers on a transatlantic jet to stop the plane and let you off in mid-flight.”

One tip drew neither agreement nor disagreement on average, and had the lowest rating in the survey.

“Shun mirrors,” Bieberman wrote. “On LSD you usually look awful to yourself in the mirror, probably because your pupils are dilated, and you see all your pores. You don’t really look that bad.”

Leary and his co-authors had said the opposite in their own 1964 guide. They recommended that guides have people look in a mirror when they were struggling to return to ordinary reality.

Experiences since then have been mixed. In a 2023 study of Reddit posts about mirror-gazing on psilocybin mushrooms, about one in ten people reported feeling good. About one in twenty reported feeling bad.

Kruger’s team suggested that Bieberman and Leary may have weighed the same trade-off differently, one putting more value on preventing harm and the other on gaining benefits.

Psychedelics are being studied as treatments for severe PTSD and depression, Kruger said. Classic psychedelics are still illegal in the United States, but Oregon and Colorado have set up state-regulated programs for supervised therapeutic use.

Most psychedelic use still happens outside those settings, the authors wrote.

In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, the most common reasons people gave for seeking emergency care after using psychedelics were the “wrong setting” and the “wrong mindset.”

Several of Bieberman’s tips, from picking a familiar room to clearing your mind of negative emotions, dealt with exactly those two things.

Agreement isn’t evidence that advice works. Everyone answered once, about tips they might give a first-timer, and the study didn’t follow anyone who used the advice.

The survey was online and in English, and most people who took it lived in North America. They were recruited through psychedelic networks, so they may not represent users worldwide. However, the authors wrote that they do resemble the readers for whom Bieberman wrote.

Stronger evidence could come from trials that test specific practices, the authors wrote, as long as no participant is denied essential safety information.

“It’s a freight train coming down the tracks,” Kruger said of the psychedelic medicines he expects to reach the market. “So, we better have a train station to safely load passengers into this train or else they’re just going to try to jump on board while this train is moving.”

Bieberman’s pamphlet said little about the days after a trip, beyond keeping the next one free. Future surveys could ask how today’s users see her other writing on that stage, the authors wrote.

The full study was published in the journal Psychedelics.

#6421. Some Evidence Suggests Amelia Earhart Was Eaten by Crabs. The Twist: She Could Have Eaten Them to Survive.

The crustaceans of Nikumaroro may have been the aviator’s best source of food—and the reason almost nothing remained of her.

If there’s one thing we love at Popular Mechanics, it’s a scientific hypothesis with enough meat on its bones to nourish a deeply-rooted psychological obsession. So it’s not surprising that one of our favorite stories focuses on the question of what might have happened if Amelia Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), following the disappearance of their plane over the Pacific Ocean in 1937.

In particular, one prominent, longstanding theory posits that the famous aviator indeed was stranded on the island, and that she eventually perished there. But her body was never found because her remains were subsequently eaten—and her bones scattered—by the giant coconut crabs (Birgus latro) that live in great profusion on the atoll.

But that raises a question. If you’re stranded on a remote Pacific island that’s jam-packed full of thousands of crabs, wouldn’t you try to eat them, instead of the other way around? Which brings us to another question.

Well, the answer to that one is pretty simple: oh yeah, absolutely! Coconut crabs are generally quite edible—in fact, they’re considered a highly prized delicacy in many Pacific island cultures. But eating them comes with significant safety warnings.

So if you’re considering eating a coconut crab, here’s what you need to know before going through with it.

First, they’re protected by conservation laws in most places where they’re found, so don’t poach them! But the flavor is fantastic. The meat is famously sweet, and it’s often compared to a very dense, firm lobster. The fat sac (the hepatopancreas) in the crab’s abdomen is particularly prized: It’s often said to have a rich, nutty, coconut-like flavor. But that delicious coconut flavor isn’t a genetic trait—it comes from their diet. Coconut crabs are opportunistic scavengers, and the fat sac functions as a storage organ. If a wild crab has recently been surviving on a diet of, say, dead birds, rotting wood, and other crabs’ molted shells, its fat will still be rich, buttery, and oily, but it won’t taste like coconut.

That’s one of the reasons why people typically capture these crabs alive, keep them penned up, and feed them an exclusive diet of coconuts for several weeks before cooking them up. This process infuses the fat sac with that highly prized, sweet coconut flavor everybody talks about.

But even more importantly, deliberately feeding the crabs a special diet flushes out any toxins that might ordinarily have built up in their flesh. The poisonous sea mango tree (Cerbera manghas) grows in exactly the same places where you’re most likely to find coconut crabs.

Both species share the same geographic distribution from the western Indian Ocean far into the South Pacific, including Kiribati, where Earhart was theoretically marooned. Coconut crabs spend most of their adult lives foraging in the same coastal scrub forests and beach thickets where sea mangoes grow. Because this ecological overlap is so common across thousands of miles of ocean, the cultural practice of penning and “purging” coconut crabs on a safe diet before eating them evolved independently across multiple different island nations. Eating a toxic crab can cause severe cardiac problems, and even death.

The answer is most definitely yes, because without sea mango trees, the main source of potential toxicity is eliminated. Nikumaroro is in a very remote area of Kiribati called the Phoenix Islands, a chain of coral atolls that often experience severe, multi-year droughts. It’s simply too dry there for the sea mango, which loves moisture, to survive. Instead, the crabs on Nikumaroro get their food from three sources: coconut palms, which were left over from failed British colonization and plantation attempts in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; Pisonia grandis (Buka) trees that can grow up to 50 feet tall, providing rotting wood and organic matter; and native coastal scrub plants like Cordia (kanawa trees), Scaevola, and Pandanus, which provide fleshy fruits for the crabs to eat.

In short, the giant crabs on Nikumaroro enjoy a diet that undoubtedly makes them beautifully flavorful when eaten. So Nikumaroro’s giant crabs could certainly have provided an abundant, safe—and delicious—source of food for Earhart and Noonan.

However, surviving on coconut crabs would have presented them with severe practical challenges. Here’s how their coconut crab situation probably would have played out.

First, there’s the challenge of catching the crabs. Coconut crabs are enormous, heavily armored, and nocturnal. More importantly, their pincers have a crushing force comparable to the bite of a lion or a bear. Trying to catch, subdue, and kill a coconut crab without proper weapons or traps, especially while weakened by dehydration or starvation, would have been extremely difficult and dangerous. A pinch could easily break a finger or cause a severe, infection-prone laceration. Plus you really have to watch your back at night when you’re trying to sleep, so you’d probably be hunting them while very tired.

Second, you need to cook the crabs. Raw crab carries a high risk of bacterial infection and parasites, so the castaways would have been obliged to build fires to cook them. And as it turns out, there’s circumstantial evidence that they might have done just that. In the early 2000s, researchers from TIGHAR (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery) performed excavations on Nikumaroro at a location called the “Seven Site.” They discovered the remains of small campfires there, and in the ashes, they found the cooked bones of birds, fish, and turtles. So there’s little doubt that someone did successfully cook local wildlife there at some point in time.

The final issue is that the most famous association between Amelia Earhart and the Nikumaroro coconut crabs isn’t that she ate them, but that they likely ate her.

TIGHAR's leading hypothesis for why Earhart's complete skeleton was never found is that after she died of starvation or exposure, the island’s massive population of coconut crabs scavenged her remains. The crabs are known to swarm dead bodies and carry bones deep into their underground burrows or into the coral rubble. The TIGHAR researchers argued that this aligns with the fact that only 13 human bones were discovered on the island in 1940, instead of a full skeleton. (The bones, alas, were subsequently lost).

So while Nikumaroro’s giant crabs could unquestionably have provided safe, high-calorie meals for a castaway with a fire and a club or spear made from local wood, the crabs were ultimately much better equipped to survive the island than Earhart was. The most likely winner of a theoretical Earhart vs. coconut crabs survival competition was, with little doubt, the crabs.

Shawn Gorman is Deputy Editor of News for Popular Mechanics. Before joining Pop Mech, he specialized in academic reading for educational testing. His diverse academic background also includes time spent as a lecturer and librarian at institutions such as the University of Kentucky, SUNY, and Harvard University. Shawn holds a Ph.D. in Modern Foreign Languages and Literatures from Boston University, an M.A. from The Ohio State University, and a B.A. in History from the University of Oregon. His favorite subjects to explore include computer science, physics, math, and biology. He lives on a medium-sized cat ranch in Easton, Pennsylvania, with his wife and two daughters.

#6420. Van Gogh’s Starry Night shows a real night sky, study suggests

For decades, art historians and astronomers have wondered whether the sky of Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night shows real stars or imagined ones. A new study argues the stars are real — and that Van Gogh likely saw them a month later than most scholars thought.

The study, published Oct. 22 in Scientific Reports, comes from a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of the South Korean telescope maker SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University’s School of Space Research in Yongin.

By combining astronomical data, historical primary sources, and statistical analysis, the team narrowed the celestial alignments shown in the painting’s sky to a handful of late-July mornings.

They further suggest Van Gogh likely painted the eastern sky as seen from his asylum room in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, around 3 a.m. on July 22, 1889. That morning, a waning crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades — the V-shaped star cluster in Taurus the Bull — were all gathered in the same small patch of sky.

RELATED: Exploring the solar system through space art

In May 1889, Van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, a former monastery outside Saint-Rémy. The previous December, after a falling-out with fellow painter Paul Gauguin, he had cut off his left ear, and more breakdowns followed. At the asylum he kept working, producing some 150 paintings, including famous works like Almond Blossom and The Starry Night.

On June 18, he wrote to his brother Theo that he had begun “a new study of a starry sky.” For most scholars, that line anchored the painting to the mid-June sky.

In 1984, art historian Albert Boime argued the painting likely shows the dawn of June 19, with the constellation Aries at its center. Two years later, astronomer Charles Whitney used weather records to rule out the 19th and suggested the sky was actually a composite. With the two theories at odds, the idea that Van Gogh painted real stars faded to what the authors call a “marginal minority view.” Most scholars granted only that the bright point near the horizon was likely Venus.

Kim’s team thought the stars were most likely real, and that the early studies were incomplete. No one had tested the painter’s field of view, the shape of its pattern of stars, and the historical record together. Plus, on the morning of June 19, the Moon was a waning gibbous, past half and nothing like the slim crescent depicted on the canvas.

Rather than assuming a date, the researchers asked whether the sky Van Gogh painted could occur, and when. Their method has two core steps. First, they compare a painted sky with astronomical simulations to see whether its arrangement is even possible. Then, they use a statistical method that measures the similarity between two shapes — called Procrustes analysis — to see how faithfully the painting’s star patterns matched real ones. When more historical data is available, the team also works to reconstruct the artist’s field of view from the landscape and check candidate dates against weather records and letters.

As a proof of concept, they applied the method to a handful of other night paintings. A 2011 study had argued that the stars in German painter Adam Elsheimer’s 1609 The Flight into Egypt weren’t copied from a single real sky, and the team’s test agreed. The painting’s Big Dipper sits at an angle to the Milky Way that never occurs in the night sky.

French painter Jean-François Millet’s Starry Night, painted between 1850 and 1865, has no letters, weather records, or known painting site to draw on, so the team ran only the core astronomical tests. The painting’s depiction of Orion — including the bright star Rigel — and Sirius revealed the tightest fit of any painting in the study to an actual star pattern.

Van Gogh’s own 1888 Starry Night Over the Rhône and Café Terrace at Night were next. Because their painting sites in Arles still stand and his letters and local weather records survive, they got the full treatment. The Big Dipper in Starry Night Over the Rhône matched the real sky with what the authors call “relative precision,” and the Summer Triangle in Café Terrace at Night fit even more closely.

RELATED: How Galileo blended science and art before his death 380 years ago

Then came The Starry Night. Van Gogh is thought to have based the painting’s village on an earlier sketch he had completed of Saint-Rémy. After locating a ridge near the asylum whose view matches the drawing, the team found the sketch captures a zoomed-in slice of the landscape. Measured diagonally, from one corner of the frame to the opposite corner, the field of view spans about 18°. They then made an assumption: that Van Gogh likely framed the painting’s night sky the same way. If he did, there should be a morning on record when the Moon, Venus, and a recognizable star pattern all fit inside that narrow frame and are arranged as painted.

Only three dawns in June and July 1889 put the Moon above Venus, as in the painting, inside that field of view: June 23, July 22, and July 23. Only the July mornings also placed the Hyades in view, and on July 22, the Moon and Venus sat in opposite corners with the cluster in between.

At the center of the canvas, a cluster of stars forms a lopsided V that closely resembles the shape of the Hyades cluster. But any handful of dots can coincidentally look like a V. The team had to evaluate whether these stars were intentionally painted as the Hyades or just happened to resemble the cluster’s shape.

They reasoned that if Van Gogh had painted the real cluster, each painted star should have a real counterpart in the same spot. That is, the star at the point of the painted V should match the star at the point of the real V, and so on down each arm of the cluster. Matching them up that way should give a better fit than any other possible combination. So the team tried every possible way of pairing the five painted stars with the five real ones — 120 combinations in all — and measured how well each fit. The natural, point-to-point pairing was the most accurate.

The match was close, but it wasn’t perfect. Of all the paintings the team tested, The Starry Night fit its stars with the lowest statistical accuracy. The authors also acknowledge that a close shape match alone can’t identify a star group. Some other constellations score as well or better and are ruled out only by other evidence, such as where they sat in the sky that morning. Nevertheless, the combined evidence still suggested July 22 as the most likely date.

One objection to this scenario remained. Historians have long held that a severe seizure in mid-July left Van Gogh unable to work. But after rereading his letters alongside weather records from that summer, the team argues the seizure may have struck later, in the last week of July, leaving Van Gogh free to watch the dawn sky on July 22.

The authors argue that the fact that so many clues converge on one morning makes it “hard to reconcile with the premise that the sky on the canvas is an arbitrary creation.” The simpler explanation is that the painting’s sky is rooted in actual observations of the sky on that morning in July — and the burden of proof now falls on anyone who says Van Gogh invented it.

Because the core test needs nothing but the star positions, the team argues it could be turned on other night paintings, including many no one has yet examined. “I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-Rémy paintings, and at Van Gogh’s movements that summer,” Kim said in a statement. “Our conversation with Van Gogh’s other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one.”

Stellarium, the free planetarium software the team used to cross-check its simulations, lets you simulate the night sky from any place and date. Enter Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, and set the clock to a couple hours before sunrise on July 22, 1889. If the sky looks too bright, turn off the atmosphere in the view settings (or press the keyboard shortcut, A).

Then search for the Hyades cluster. Brilliant Venus sits on one side, a slim crescent Moon slightly higher on the other, and between them the V of the Hyades. You can scroll through the hours to watch the scene wheel up from the horizon before dawn. Then step back a day to July 21, or ahead to July 23 and 24, and watch the Moon slide toward Venus. Or compare the view with June 19, the date Boime proposed, and judge for yourself which sky best fits the canvas.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6419. Decades of research show just how much wild animals depend on insects for food, shelter and medicine

Moths feed algae in sloth fur, parrots live in termite mounds, and ants arm poison frogs. So, insect decline is costing wildlife more than just meals.

Brown-throated sloths carry moths in their fur, and the moths help feed them. The insects leave nitrogen behind, which feeds algae growing in the fur, and the sloths eat the algae.

Once a month, a sloth climbs down to the forest floor to leave its droppings, and the moths lay their eggs in them.

A new review of hundreds of studies finds partnerships like this all over the animal world. Animals with backbones, from bats to frogs, depend on insects for shelter, protection and cleanup, not only for meals.

When insects decline, the authors conclude, many of those animals are likely to suffer.

Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, led the work.

She shared the lead with Rob Cooke of the U.K. Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) and Chris Elphick of the University of Connecticut. Members of the team spanned eight countries.

It’s a review, so they gathered decades of other scientists’ findings rather than collecting new field data.

“We often hear about their importance as pollinators, or decomposers, or food for insectivores like birds and bats, but we forget about all the other things they do for us and for other species,” Grames said.

Food is the best-documented link. The team pulled together diet records for 19,750 species of land and freshwater animals with backbones, about two in five of all such species.

Of those, 73 percent eat insects or other invertebrates, meaning animals without a backbone, such as spiders and worms, and 44 percent eat nothing else.

Those records are lopsided. Diets are on file for 95 percent of bird species, but for only 4 percent of ray-finned fish species.

Birds need insects most when they breed. Of North America’s land birds, 96 percent raise their chicks partly or entirely on insects. Purple martins alone eat an estimated 412 billion insects a year.

Other animals binge. A Couch’s spadefoot toad can eat more than half its body weight in termites at a single feeding, enough calories to last it a year. Diets built on ants and termites have evolved again and again.

Some animals use insects to get other food. Certain herons and egrets set insects on the water’s surface to lure fish. Kangaroo rats raid lines of harvester ants and steal the seeds the ants are carrying.

Termite mounds and ant nests tend to hold steady temperatures and are well ventilated, which makes them good shelters. Small mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians all use termite mounds when they breed.

Hooded parrots live inside them. White-throated round-eared bats dig out and maintain cavities in termite mounds, using a kind of scent camouflage to fend off attacks.

Frogs, salamanders and reptiles use ant nests to escape predators. Some also move in during dry seasons, because the humidity inside stays steady.

Some frogs, lizards and snakes lay their eggs in ant nests, and in some cases fungus-growing ants groom the eggs and cover them with material from their fungus gardens.

Other animals reuse what insects leave behind. Some bats move into abandoned holes made by longhorn beetle larvae.

Many birds use spider and insect silk in their nests, which strengthens them, keeps them warm and helps hide them. Bowerbirds decorate the structures they build to attract mates with butterfly wings and beetle parts.

Living near stinging insects can pay off. Many small birds build their nests close to wasps, ants or other stinging insects, and experiments suggest that choice helps more nests succeed.

Other animals take the insects’ chemical weapons for themselves. Pitohui birds carry toxins that come from the melyrid beetles they eat, and those toxins likely deter ticks and predators. Some snakes eat firefly larvae and store the toxins.

Amphibians probably do it more than any other group. Scientists have detected more than 800 defensive chemicals in amphibian skin, and most of them come from insects in the diet.

In some toxic poison frogs, ants make up 50 to 73 percent of what they eat, while ants are a much smaller part of the diet for their harmless relatives.

That means a frog’s chemical defenses depend partly on which insects are around to eat. When the available prey changes, the mix of toxins in its skin can change too.

Chimpanzees apply insects to open wounds, though scientists don’t know which chemicals are involved or what the treatment does.

More than 200 bird species use ants to groom themselves, a habit called anting. Proposed reasons include removing parasites, easing skin irritation and keeping feathers in good shape.

Insects also clean up. In hooded parrot nests, a moth lives alongside the chicks and eats their droppings. Moths in owl and kingfisher nests break down fur, crushed feathers and leftover pellets.

The arrangement is old: a beetle was feeding on shed feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period.

Dung beetles help on a bigger scale. By drying out dung and letting air into it, they leave fewer parasites alive inside.

Where antiparasitic drugs, such as ivermectin, are given to livestock dung beetle communities have been devastated, and much less dung gets removed. What that means for disease in wild animals isn’t well studied.

The relationship isn’t all help. Mosquitoes spread avian malaria, which affects bird species worldwide, and mantids occasionally catch hummingbirds.

Researchers studying insect losses have mostly asked what happens to the food supply, and some of the numbers are stark.

Across Europe, insect-eating birds declined by 13 percent from 1990 to 2015, while birds with mixed diets held steady. Of the 3 billion birds North America has lost since 1970, 2.9 billion came from species that rely on insects for at least part of their lives.

That doesn’t prove the insects caused it. Bird, bat and insect declines don’t always line up on a map, and they may be separate responses to the same environmental pressures.

A pooled analysis of 125 studies did link more insect prey to birds raising more young, with chicks in better condition.

The risk is sharper for picky eaters like the Critically Endangered mountain pygmy possum, which times its breeding around the bogong moth. After the moth’s steep decline over the past decade, the possum’s shrinking food supply is now a primary threat.

The extinction of the Eskimo curlew has been blamed in part on the loss of the Rocky Mountain locust, a large part of its diet. “If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

The team checked its diet records against the IUCN Red List, the global record of species at risk. Of the 622 Critically Endangered species in those records, 202 eat only invertebrates, so their survival depends on having enough of them.

Yet the Red List assessments for those species say little about insect decline as a main cause. Most threatened species lack detailed diet records, and losing food is tangled up with losing habitat.

Most insect species haven’t been formally described. Many diet studies lump insects together with spiders, worms and other invertebrates. And experiments that start with the insects and follow the effects up to the animals that eat them are lacking.

The review came out of the Status of Insects research network. The authors call for shared standards for recording which insects animals eat and use.

They also favor closer work between researchers who study animals with backbones and those who are insect specialists. Citizen science photos and DNA traces from the environment could also help.

Until that data exists, researchers can’t reliably rank which of these thousands of partnerships animals can least afford to lose.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Reviews Biodiversity.
