Scientists in the U.S. and Canada are decoding grizzly bears' behavior to learn how they navigate a human-dominated world. What they find could build a safer future for both species.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Across 53 challenging days between fall 2020 and spring 2021, a 360-pound (160 kilograms) young male grizzly bear nicknamed "Lingenpolter" tried to cross Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times. High-resolution GPS tracking showed him moving parallel to four lanes of roaring traffic, bouncing off the highway like a furry pinball as he searched for a gap.

Eventually, Lingenpolter beat the odds, probably by slipping under a river bridge. But his hero's journey shows what a formidable barrier a busy highway can be for wildlife, Cecily Costello, a research wildlife biologist at Montana's Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks, told Live Science. "It is easy to imagine the difficulty this grizzly bear experienced trying to reach the other side," Costello said.

A map of all the places Lingenpolter attempted to cross the road before making it across.

This past May, another grizzly wasn't so lucky. Braving a crossing near one of Lingenpolter's attempts, the 27-year-old male bear was struck and killed by a truck, triggering a multicar rollover.

It's crucial for grizzly bears (Ursus arctos), also known as brown bears, to have room to roam. When they can't move between populations to mate, small groups get genetically isolated. And what's true for bears can also be true for other wildlife. "It's really challenging to be a small, fragmented population," said Michael Proctor, a wildlife biologist at Birchdale Ecological Ltd., a Canada-based environmental consulting firm. Such fragmentation is "one of the mechanisms by which we lose entire communities, and sometimes whole species," he told Live Science.

Nowhere is this challenge more urgent than in the 2,100 mile long (3,400 kilometers) region stretching along the spine of the Rocky Mountains between Yellowstone in Wyoming and the Yukon in northern Canada. The area, which spans five U.S. states, two Canadian provinces, and more than 75 Indigenous territories "represents the most intact, connected, wild, large mountain region in the world," Jordan Reeves, program director of landscape connectivity at the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y), which aims to secure connectivity throughout the region told Live Science.

The terrain between Yellowstone and the Yukon is the most intact wild large mountain region, and is crucial for bear migration.

But as highways, rail lines, and human development fragment its valleys, maintaining connected pathways for grizzly bears across this landscape has become a challenge.

Grizzlies range across vast, diverse terrain, spanning high-elevation alpine habitats, mid-mountain slopes, and low valley bottoms, which means safeguarding their movement can also protect passageways for coexisting species, including wolverines, mountain goats, elk and bighorn sheep, Proctor said. That's why researchers are trying to understand why, where and when grizzlies move. And what stops them in their tracks.

"We're looking at how a bear sees the world," Andrew Derocher, a bear biologist at the University of Alberta who has used GPS collars on grizzly bears to trace their movements, told Live Science.

When Sarah Sells started her graduate studies in animal behavior, her supervisor told her to "try to crawl into their fur brains and understand how they think," Sells told Live Science. Although we can't recreate exactly what's going on between a grizzly's ears, GPS collars that track animal movement hourly can tell scientists a lot about how animals behave, said Sells, who is currently the assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey's Montana Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit.

That tracking data is starting to produce an incredibly detailed picture not just of where bears go but also how and why they're making those choices.

"Bears are food finding machines," Chris Servheen, a bear biologist with the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Bear Specialist Group, told Live Science. "So remembering where they found food is critical to their success in life."

Using a combination of telemetry data (information collected by tracking devices) and movement modeling, Derocher and colleagues have investigated how well grizzlies remember where food is and when it is best to visit a foraging patch. Derocher's research showed that about two-thirds of the bears have a great memory for where and in what season they previously found food. His tracking data also revealed that wild bears generally avoid humans. But bears have only a few months to fatten up for winter. If food is scarce, many bears go into human environments and sometimes get killed, Proctor said.

The data is also offering insight into different bear "personalities." Bears are ultimately individuals, with their own traits and quirks, Servheen said.

A young male bear named Lingenpolter tried to cross the Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times before successfully making it across.

Tracking data suggests that a lot of bear behavior is transmitted culturally via a mother's influence. Sometimes, the wrong behavior can get passed down to the next generation, Servheen said. For example, an infamous female grizzly known as 399 jaywalked potentially hundreds of times in the Jackson Hole valley in Wyoming while managing to keep her distance from humans. Her 20-odd cubs learned to follow her example, but they lacked her strategic caution. Several were killed by vehicles or management euthanizations.

"It's a risky thing to teach your kids to do stuff like that," Servheen said. "And her offspring weren't as smart as she was."

Further north along the region between Yellowstone and the Yukon, Proctor's first DNA survey across 1,500 square miles (4,000 square kilometers) of southern British Columbia in the late 1990s shattered his illusion that the bears, along with bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) and other species in this province, were free to roam. Instead, he found a "cracked windshield" landscape, where roads and human sprawl had fractured the wilderness into isolated genetic islands. In the 2000s, the genetic diversity of the South Selkirk grizzly bears — a detatched subpopulation inhabiting southeastern British Columbia, northern Idaho, and northeastern Washington — was so low, for example, that biologists feared the bears wouldn't survive.

But Proctor and his colleagues went on to use bear movement data to model pathways through human-settled valleys. Proctor was so convinced about the viability of one potential corridor that he paid 10,000 Canadian dollars ($7,000) of his own money to buy a key piece of land right in the middle of it. "That was the first canoe over the waterfall of purchasing connectivity land," Proctor said

Proctor’s land secured a segment of a crucial connectivity corridor and, in the following years, he and other scientists partnered with trusts to purchase other land parcels, build fences, and establish safe corridors for grizzlies in the Creston Valley in southeastern British Columbia. These actions helped bears move north and south (sometimes across the border) and between the South Selkirk Mountains and Purcell Mountains. The researchers then watched bears like "Captain Hook," who'd been shot in the leg, hobble into the South Selkirks and breed with eight females. By 2021, nine immigrant bears had produced 27 new offspring within the population.

"This is gene flow; this is connectivity," Proctor said. "We took a completely isolated population and pretty much recovered it."

The peaks of the Purcell and Rocky Mountain ranges frame the Rocky Mountain Trench insoutheastern British Columbia—a core component of the Yellowstone to Yukon region. Steeptopography forces both wildlife and human activity into the same low-elevation valley bottoms.

Despite efforts to safeguard corridors through human occupied landscape, roads continue to stop bears in their tracks. When Servheen tracked bears near Highway 2 in northwest Montana, he found that many of the grizzlies avoided the highway altogether and those that crossed did so at night. But he also found that the bears' crossings clustered in specific sections of the road. Finding the crossing zones has helped researchers identify good locations for constructing overpasses and underpasses on many busy highways, but a crossing structure on its own is not enough, Servheen cautioned.

A bear's memory for where to find food is exemplary, but there's no special reward in a bear's brain for crossing a road safely — only a fatal penalty when they don't, Servheen said. So conservationists can't rely on bears to remember where crossings are. Instead, they must build fencing along the highway to funnel wildlife into the underpasses or overpasses. Then, the immediate land on each side needs to allow animals safe passage. "Otherwise, you have a bridge to nowhere," Servheen said.

Now researchers such as Sells are trying to use data about bears' likeliest routes to determine potential corridors in locations where they have little tracking data or where few bears live yet.

To do this, Sells is developing a virtual "Sims for Bears" that recreates the Continental Divide Ecosystem in Montana. In the life-simulation video game "The Sims," players give virtual humans personality traits, preferences and needs, and then drop them into a virtual environment to see how they behave.

Sells built the model using the GPS collaring data from 65 grizzly bears navigating individual paths through greenery, riparian areas and around forests and roads. Then, she "parachutes" an individual digital bear into a detailed computer simulation of real-world terrain and has them take thousands of virtual steps. By running these multiple simulated bears through thousands of iterations across the digital terrain, the researchers can watch where the virtual bears repeatedly choose to walk, effectively creating a map of predicted movement corridors.

Sells has used the model to predict how grizzly bears might recolonize the Bitterroot ecosystem of Idaho and Montana, which Lingenpolter was heading toward when attempting to cross Interstate 90.

To get to the Bitterroot Mountains, bears must pass through a valley filled with people, roads, garbage and fruit trees. "So knowing where they are more likely to end up is helpful to address things that could be difficult for humans or bears," Sells told Live Science.

The data is also confirming that the greatest barrier bears face comes from human contact or transportation infrastructure across the entire Yellowstone-to-Yukon region. Studies from across west-central North America report that humans directly or indirectly caused between 77% and 90% of grizzly bear deaths from 1989 to 2015. Hunting, managed kills in urban areas and road and rail collisions all take a toll.

Bears running across the road in Glacier National Park.

Bears in the wild usually avoid people, but some bears seek out human-dominated areas because they know these places are a source of food. People move to the Elk Valley in southeastern British Columbia because they love nature, but then they plant apple trees in their backyard, which attract bears, said Clayton Lamb, a wildlife scientist at the nonprofit Biodiversity Pathways.

Quickly, a bear eating backyard apples gets labeled a "problem bear," "when really it is a 'people problem,'" Lamb told Live Science.

Even human recreation takes a toll on bears' health and ability to move freely. Lamb's research has shown that grizzly bears try to avoid areas next to busy cycling and hiking trails.

To minimize human-bear conflict, Michelle McLellan, a wildlife ecologist at Biodiversity Pathways, has tracked trail use by both people and grizzlies in the West Kootenay region of British Columbia. McLellan documented people's habits using trail cameras and apps such as Strava Metro. Her research shows that the bears use the trails to move quickly between foraging spots but have learned not to use the trails that are most popular with humans. Consequently, the Nelson Cycling Club decided to close certain trails in the spring and cautioned riders about when and how to use the open trails. "Ride aware, make noise, slow down when needed," the club cautioned in its May newsletter.

Working with information from McLellan, the club has cut back overgrown vegetation along sight lines to prevent mountain bikers from startling bears at close range. They've also constructed wooden platforms on sections of trails that clatter and rumble as bikes pass over them, giving bears early notice of approaching riders. "The key is to not surprise them by making a lot of noise." McLellan told Live Science, noting that grizzlies are more likely to attack if they are surprised.

One advantage of having human mountain biking and hiking trails concentrated close to towns is that it focuses recreation into specific areas, Lamb said. Keeping trails condensed supplies multiple accessible paths and reduces humans encroaching on true wilderness — prime bear habitat. "The goal would be to ensure that there's sufficient recreation opportunities for people to stay healthy and connected to their local landscape while ensuring that wildlife can still move around and access their habitats," Lamb said

As humans increasingly live, work and play in bear territory, it's important to recognize the impact on the animals, Servheen said. "The bears never get a day off," he said. "Every day, they're trying to stay away from people and make a living in a place with multiple people on the landscape."

Bears expend a lot of much-needed energy trying to avoid people, and they won't be able to do that forever, Servheen said. As humans increase the development of private lands and recreation in bear territory, the squeeze is on. "There's going to be more conflicts with bears, and more dead bears," Servheen said.

The bears have done their part, Lamb said. His research has shown that bears living near humans are adapting by becoming mostly nocturnal, which reduces their odds of clashing with humans. "So, we need to meet them where they are at and see what we can do to share the space," Lamb said.

On the human side, people need to make it less tempting for bears to be in human dominated areas, McLellan said. That means keeping garbage stowed and making sure there is no ripe fruit available. "If you live rurally, you want them to be able to pass through your property but not linger near your home or in your front yard," McLellan said.

Bears have proved to be adaptable and persistent; Lingenpolter tried to cross the highway dozens of times before finding a way under. However, Servheen warned that we are putting them in a tough spot. To keep bear populations stable, scientists need data on bear behavior to help inform land management policies that create safe pathways for grizzlies to move through human dominated areas and regulate recreation with bears in mind, Servheen said.

"If we want to have bears in the future, we need to think about the needs bears have for some level of space on the landscape," Servheen said.

Securing that space across the vast Yellowstone to Yukon landscape requires more than just land acquisitions and highway overpasses — it requires increasing public awareness and counteracting the perception that bears are inherently aggressive and irrational, Proctor said. If people understand bear behavior, they can learn to act in ways that neither attract bears nor threaten them. And understanding the totality of bears’ strong drive to survive, and protect each other, can elicit empathy and motivation to protect this iconic species.

Early in his career, Proctor captured, immobilized and radio-collared a mother grizzly with her two yearlings, or newly adolescent bears. While the research team worked, the young bears circled quietly at a distance. When the scientists finally stepped back and the mother began to stir, the yearlings approached cautiously. As the mother's groggy head rested on a log, the yearlings' long-clawed front paws delicately explored the radio collar. Then, each one rested its head directly on hers, to form a quiet pile of three bear heads.

"They just wanted to touch mom after this ordeal," Proctor said. "Yes, grizzlies can be rough and dangerous but they can also be gentle at times," Proctor said.

#6417. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 5: Smoke out the Southern Cigar

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tonight’s target is a bit of a test: How far south can you see? At a latitude of 40° north, NGC 55 in Sculptor — also called the Southern Cigar Galaxy or the String of Pearls Galaxy — only rises about 10° above the southern horizon at its highest, which occurs around 9 P.M. local time. Observers farther south will see it higher in the sky, while those farther north will see it closer to the horizon or be unable to make it out at all.

For those observers who can catch it, NGC 55 is a bright, 8th-magnitude edge-on barred spiral located just under 4° northwest of magnitude 2.4 Alpha (α) Phoenicis in Phoenix, which sits below the galaxy as you look south around this time of night. This galaxy is not only bright, it’s quite large, stretching roughly the width of the Full Moon (½°) at its longest. It is quite thin, however, only some 6’ wide along the other dimension. You’ll immediately see that its nucleus is not in the center, but offset to the west. Several other bright knots of star formation may also be visible within the galaxy’s plane — particularly if you drop in a nebula filter.

#6416. Dirty air actually breaks down the smell of flowers and stops bees and moths from finding their food

Ozone and nitrogen oxides cut pollinators' ability to find flowers by about half, and ozone will stay high until around 2050 as fuels change.

A bee finds a flower the way you find a bakery, by following the smell. Exhaust from cars and machines breaks those scent molecules apart in the air.

A review of 22 experiments now puts a number on the damage. Polluted air cut how well pollinators found and used flowers by roughly half, and two pollutants together cut it by more than two thirds.

The surprise is in the timing. Even as the world burns less fossil fuel, one of those two pollutants, ozone, isn’t expected to drop below today’s levels until after about 2050.

James Ryalls at the University of Reading led the review with colleagues Jacob Bishop and Carol Wagstaff. In an interview with Earth.com, Ryalls said the result that surprised him most was what the two gases did together.

“It was the first time this interaction had been quantified for pollinators,” he said.

Flowers advertise with chemicals that drift off their petals, and pollinators follow those chemicals to the food. Ozone and nitrogen oxides react with the scent molecules in the air. They break some down and change others, so the trail an insect is following gets weaker and stranger.

Researchers have also linked the gases to duller antennae, poorer learning and memory, and weaker colonies in bees. However, the review ranks that direct damage behind the scent damage.

Ozone is a gas that forms in sunlit air from other pollutants. Nitrogen oxides come mostly from engines, and diesel engines above all.

Ryalls’s team pulled together every experiment it could find that measured flower pollinators in clean air against polluted air. There were 22 studies in all, with 87 comparisons between them.

Most used honeybees or bumblebees. A few used a hawkmoth, a fig wasp or a mix of wild insects, and the setups ranged from lab chambers to greenhouses to open fields with pollutants piped in.

Across those studies, increased ozone lowered pollinator performance by an average of 42 percent, and increased nitrogen oxides lowered it by 46 percent.

Performance here covers three things: how well insect pollinators found flowers, how well they fed on them, and how many turned up.

Only three research teams tested both gases at once, and in those experiments the average loss was 68 percent. That is worse than either gas alone, but well short of the 88 percent you would get by simply adding the two. The gases don’t stack.

Ryalls had an explanation for the gap. “This reflects real atmospheric chemistry, where ozone and nitrogen oxides can partially react with and offset each other,” he told Earth.com.

In the three studies that measured each gas and the pair against the same clean-air control, the extra harm from adding the second gas was smaller still.

The damage was not spread evenly across what insects do. Searching efficiency, the measure of how well a pollinator locates flowers, fell by 67 percent on average. Feeding, once an insect reached a flower, and the number of insects present changed little.

Ryalls said he wanted people to notice that pattern. The insects were not sickened so much as lost.

Specialists have it worst. A bee that visits many kinds of flower can switch cues when one scent breaks down. An insect tied to one plant, like the tobacco hawkmoth or the yucca moth, has no backup.

Timing matters too. Ozone peaks in daylight, when bees and butterflies are out. That is bad timing for crops such as almonds and oilseed rape, whose flowers open in daylight when ozone peaks.

In contrast, nitrogen oxides are often highest at night, when moths do their pollinating. So the two groups face different pollutants, and cutting one gas doesn’t protect both.

Burning less fossil fuel cuts nitrogen oxides. Ozone, however, is made in the air from several ingredients, including methane and carbon monoxide, and those stay high for longer.

Under the middle-of-the-road emissions path used by the IPCC, the authors expect ground-level ozone to stay elevated through mid-century and only drop below today’s levels after about 2050.

On a high-emissions path, ozone is predicted to keep rising into the 2060s. It will only fall below today’s levels near the end of the century.

Diesel vehicles complicate the picture further, because a diesel sold today can stay on the road for more than 20 years. Britain’s decision to push its ban on new gasoline and diesel cars from 2030 to 2035 is the kind of delay the authors said will stretch the hard years out.

One oddity cuts the other way: in cities, nitrogen oxides break down some of the ozone, a buffer that fades in the countryside where there is less exhaust.

“Most of the food we grow depends on healthy pollinators, so protecting them from pollution cannot wait until 2050,” Ryalls said.

Asked by Earth.com what gardeners and farmers can do, Ryalls said cutting local nitrogen oxide emissions would help most.

He suggested replacing older diesel machinery and generators, keeping high-emission equipment idle during peak flowering, expanding green spaces, and letting lawns run wild and flower.

The evidence is lopsided. Of the 22 studies, 19 were done in Europe and 16 used bees or their relatives. That matters because about 70 percent of crop species get some benefit from insect pollination. The countries with the dirtiest air, such as India and China, are the ones likely to be hit hardest.

Flies, beetles and most moths are barely tested, and the tropics, where pollution is often heavier and more insects are generalists, are almost absent from research studies.

The doses were high as well: the average ozone level in the experiments was 161 parts per billion, more than twice the U.S. limit of 70. Harm clearly happened at those levels, but the studies can’t say where it begins.

Whether it starts at a sharp threshold or builds gradually is still an open question, and so is where a safe level might be.

Ryalls wants the next experiments run where the air is already dirty. “I’d like to test these effects in higher-pollution regions and tropical systems, where baseline pollutant levels are often higher and pollinator communities differ,” he said.

His group is also testing treatments that could boost the scents flowers give off, to help insects find them in polluted air.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment.

#6415. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6414. ALS Stole His Voice—Then, a ‘Digital Twin’ Read His Thoughts And Started Speaking for Him

This technology could restore the art of conversation for people with paralysis, but questions remain about who is really in control.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Did Walter want coffee? His virtual avatar responded, but it gave an unexpected answer. Instead of nodding or signaling yes with a thumbs-up, it waved goodbye. The mistake was funny, but it illustrated a serious problem: When technology communicates on someone’s behalf, an incorrect gesture can change the meaning of an entire exchange.

Walter, who has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, knows how much can be lost when communication becomes difficult. He went from slightly slurred speech to being unintelligible within approximately six months. He eventually relied on emails, text-to-speech applications, and telephone relay services. ALS is a progressive neurological disease that damages the nerve cells responsible for voluntary muscle movement, gradually affecting a person’s ability to speak, swallow, move, and breathe. Although the disease weakens muscles, it does not necessarily impair thinking or understanding.

“Somehow you try to keep a communication going while compromising to focus on the most essential content,” Walter says. “That doesn’t leave space for emotions and gestures at all.”

Determined to find a more efficient way to communicate, Walter began researching brain-computer interfaces. After attending an ALS Association webinar about emerging technologies, he discovered that neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, at the University of California, San Francisco, was leading a study that could potentially change lives. He contacted the research team himself, undeterred by the prospect of the invasive implant it would require. With ALS shortening his life expectancy, he also saw participation as an opportunity to advance technology that might benefit future patients, even if he never lived to use a commercial version.

The team began working with Walter on the virtual avatar in early summer 2025, gradually training the system to recognize his attempted speech and movements separately before combining them. “Every step and progress was fascinating and quite unbelievable at the same time,” he recalls. But the defining moment came when the avatar successfully decoded his speech and gestures together. “What a great milestone!” he says.

The research team’s brain-computer interface (BCI) decodes attempted speech and gestures simultaneously through a single implant, translating those signals into words and movements performed by a personalized virtual avatar. Their study, published in Nature Neuroscience, offers a glimpse of technology that could eventually restore something beyond words: the expressive dimensions of human conversation.

The process of getting your own virtual avatar started with electrocorticography (ECoG), which records electrical activity from electrodes positioned over the brain’s surface. The researchers’ implant covered a broad region of the sensorimotor cortex, which is involved in controlling speech and movement. Different areas are more strongly associated with different body movements, providing clues that machine-learning models can use to distinguish attempted speech from gestures.

But the researchers encountered an unexpected complication.

“What surprised us was that models trained on speech and gestures separately didn’t work as well when participants attempted both at the same time,” Samantha Brosler, a UCSF researcher and first co-author of the study, says.

The problem involved overlapping neural activity. Some brain regions respond during both speech and gesture attempts, and their activity patterns can change when those actions occur together.

Jennifer Collinger, PhD, a neuroprosthetics researcher at the University of Pittsburgh who was not involved in the research, describes this as context-dependent neural activity. “The neural activity associated with a particular movement, such as waving, may be different depending on whether or not you are speaking at the same time,” she explains.

To address this, the UCSF team, led by neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, trained two parallel decoding models using recordings of participants attempting speech and gestures separately and together. A participant attempting to say “hello” while waving, for example, supplied neural activity that could train one model to recognize the phrase and another to recognize the movement. The combined training improved decoding performance.

Encouragingly, the models could recognize some speech-and-gesture combinations they had not encountered during training. That matters because teaching a system every possible combination of human words and movements would be impractical.

The study involved three participants with paralysis, although the main simultaneous speech-and-gesture experiments involved two. For a participant with ALS, the researchers tested 10 predefined phrases and 10 gestures. For one participant, the system recognized 10 conversational phrases, including “hello,” “thank you,” “nice to meet you,” and “how’s it going?,” alongside 10 gestures such as waving, nodding, shrugging, pointing, and shaking hands. The avatar could combine the two, allowing someone to say “hello” while waving or “nice to meet you” while extending a hand. Researchers tested all 100 possible phrase-and-gesture pairings, including combinations that would rarely occur in ordinary conversation, to assess how reliably the system could decode both actions together. During real-time testing, speech decoding reached 70 percent accuracy, and gesture decoding reached 66 percent. Offline testing for participants with paralysis following a brainstem stroke also produced valuable results.

Collinger considers the findings encouraging but emphasizes their experimental boundaries, in part because this study was limited to a finite set of speech and gesture actions. The system wasn’t generating spontaneous conversation. It recognized predefined phrases, displayed decoded speech as text, and triggered corresponding avatar animations when gestures were detected.

That distinction raises questions about user control. Walter’s accidental goodbye was amusing, but an incorrect gesture in another situation could misrepresent someone’s intentions. User feedback is essential to ensuring the technology communicates what someone actually intends, Collinger says.

Future versions could allow users to confirm or correct decoded outputs, potentially through eye tracking, Brosler says.

The system currently relies on a wired connection to external computers. An everyday user would need an overhaul that allows true freedom: wireless transmission, portability, and reduced communication delays. It must overcome multiple engineering challenges, Brosler says, such as miniaturizing parts, attaining reliable neural recordings, lowering power consumption, and reducing heat generation.

Walter has his own priorities: the human dimension of the technology’s development. “It’s a two-sided learning curve for the avatar and the patient,” he explains.

An ideal solution would decode a user’s neural cues, he says, adding that wireless mobility and less invasive technology could make such systems more attractive to users.

During one successful experimental dialogue, the system decoded Walter’s attempted speech and gestures together without error. He remembers being overwhelmed. “I was extremely moved by the avatar’s response to my ‘thoughts,’ I couldn’t help laughing uncontrollably with pure joy.”

Even with its limitations, Walter describes the personalized avatar as a digital twin whose movements reflect his intentions and personality.

For Collinger, experiences like Walter’s demonstrate why accuracy alone cannot define success. “Restoring the ability to communicate is not just measured in words per minute,” she says. Independence, relationships, community participation, and personal expression matter, too.

The UCSF experiment has not yet restored unrestricted, natural conversation. But it suggests that the future of brain-computer interfaces may depend on understanding communication as more than the transmission of words—and giving people greater control over everything those words cannot express.

#6413. Nov. 5, 2006: Mars Global Surveyor goes quiet

Designed to study Mars in a comprehensive way, examining its atmosphere, its interior, and its surface, the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) launched Nov. 7, 1996. By Sept. 12, 1997, it would reach Mars and slip into orbit around the Red Planet. Over the next nine years, it revealed an evolving world of ongoing geological dynamism, analyzed the history of water on Mars, tracked the movements of ice at its poles, and analyzed its topography and weather. With nearly 200,000 photos captured, MGS supplied more images of Mars than all the missions before it – combined. It also helped NASA plan for future rover missions to the Red Planet.

MGS substantially exceeded its two-year mission, but on Nov. 2, 2006, the orbiter signaled to NASA that it was experiencing difficulties with its solar panels. Two days without communication followed. On Nov. 5, more signals were sent, and then MGS went silent. The mission officially ended on Nov. 14, with NASA concluding a battery failure had caused a computer error that closed out MGS’s tour.

#6412. Young children are fascinated by sharks – so why are older kids more fearful?

A survey finds most children like sharks, but older kids express more fear, raising questions about how views of these animals develop.

Sharks have a scary reputation, but many young children like them. Some think they look cool, while others like the way they swim.

A survey of parents of 374 children aged two to 12 found that 69% of the children liked sharks. Older children were more likely to say sharks scared them.

Brianna Le Busque, an environmental psychologist at Adelaide University‘s School of Physics, Chemistry and Earth Sciences, led the study. Parents asked the questions and recorded their children’s answers.

“What’s really interesting is that most of the children in our study actually liked sharks, and many were fascinated by them,” Le Busque said.

People are often less willing to protect animals they fear or dislike. That makes children’s early views of sharks worth understanding.

The few earlier studies on this topic mostly found fear. In a 2020 study, five-year-olds chose a face to show how a shark photo made them feel, and most chose a fearful face.

But those studies left out toddlers. They also usually asked children about sharks alongside other animals, which may have made sharks seem less appealing next to dogs, horses and dolphins.

For the new study, 323 parents took an online survey in 2024. They asked their children what sharks do, what they look like and whether they liked them.

Parents wrote down the answers word for word and noted any hand gestures. They asked brothers and sisters separately so they couldn’t copy each other.

The team counted a child as expressing fear if they called sharks scary, said they were afraid or clearly showed fear another way.

Saying sharks bite or are dangerous didn’t count, because knowing an animal can hurt you doesn’t always mean you fear it.

The most common reason children gave for liking sharks was that they were cool. One four-year-old girl said, “sharks are very cool.”

When describing sharks, 44% mentioned teeth and 33% said they were big. Most talked about sharks swimming and eating, although about one in five said they hurt people.

Some children mixed facts with imagination. A six-year-old boy asked whether sharks were reptiles, then answered himself, “no they’re not, they’re dinosaurs.”

Children who disliked sharks most often said sharks hurt people. One 10-year-old boy explained, “because they could eat me.”

Overall, 13.9% of the children described sharks as scary or expressed fear of them.

Older children did this more often, and the team’s analysis suggested the pattern was unlikely to be due to chance.

“But as children got older, we saw an increase in associations between sharks and fear,” Le Busque said.

“That raises important questions about what children are learning about sharks as they grow up and the role that society, media and other influences might play.”

The team found no clear difference between boys and girls or between children in Australia, the U.S. and the U.K., where most participants lived. How often children went into the ocean made no clear difference either.

The survey compared different age groups. It did not follow the same children as they grew up, so it couldn’t show how any one child’s feelings changed.

Books were the most common way children had come across sharks. About 65% had read shark books or had someone read them aloud.

Another 59% had seen sharks at an aquarium, and 38% had watched TV shows featuring them. About a quarter had seen shark films, including Finding Nemo and Jaws.

Some 13% had sung “Baby Shark,” which became YouTube’s most-viewed video in 2020.

The researchers think these experiences may help explain why many children liked sharks.

Watching sharks swim among other fish at an aquarium, for example, may help children see sharks as more than dangerous animals.

Films may leave a different impression. Older children were more likely to mention Jaws, a film long linked to negative views of sharks and even government responses to shark bites.

Finding Nemo also mixes friendly and frightening images. Bruce appears as a friendly shark trying to stop eating fish, but becomes aggressive when he smells a single drop of blood.

“Sharks are often portrayed in very dramatic and sensational ways, particularly when there is a shark bite or in popular films,” Le Busque said.

Still, the study did not test whether films changed children’s feelings about sharks. The researchers say that needs more study.

Among parents, 44% reported low fear of sharks and 30% reported high fear. Many less fearful parents said they lived far from sharks or could avoid them.

One parent wrote, “The same reason I’m not afraid of earthquakes – I don’t live in an area where they reside.”

The team found no clear link between parents’ fear and their children’s fear.

Some parents said sharks weren’t an everyday threat, which may give children few chances to see their parents react fearfully.

A larger study might find a small link, the researchers noted.

Parents may have influenced their children’s answers or misunderstood them. The researchers accepted that risk because toddlers can’t complete a survey alone.

Views of sharks also differ across cultures, and shark populations vary around the world. Only 14 children in the study were 12, and none were teenagers.

Children’s fear might ease during their teens as they learn more. But strong fears that start in childhood can also last into adulthood.

A recent review found that people who know more about sharks tend to fear them less. Earlier research also linked direct experiences with sharks to greater tolerance of them.

In another study, people who swam with sharks were more likely to report helping sharks two years later.

These findings suggest that learning and positive experiences may help, though they don’t tell us how each child’s feelings will change.

The researchers suggest using lessons and media to show children the many kinds of sharks, helping balance stories built around fear.

“Children are clearly capable of seeing sharks as fascinating, interesting animals, rather than simply something to be afraid of,” Le Busque said.

“Education and positive experiences could be really important in helping children understand sharks as diverse marine animals and appreciate the important role they play in our oceans.”

To learn whether fear fades or lasts, researchers will need to follow the same children into their teens.

They also want future studies to use a standard set of questions about fear, making the results easier to compare.

The study is published in the journal Human Dimensions of Wildlife.

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

#6409. Intensive breathing exercises can create psychedelic ‘tripping’ effects by changing how the brain talks to itself

Intensive breathwork cut brain blood flow by about 45 percent in MRI scans, yet the depth of the altered state tracked brain networks, not the drop.

People who practice intensive breathwork (fast, nonstop breathing) for an hour describe something close to a psychedelic trip. They recount vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity with the universe, and no drug involved.

Inside an MRI scanner, the brain lost nearly half its usual blood supply during that experience. Yet how far the blood flow fell had nothing to do with how deep the experience went.

Christian Schmitz led the work at the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim, Germany. His colleagues came from the Medical Faculty Mannheim of Heidelberg University and the MIND Foundation in Berlin.

His team scanned the brains of 30 experienced breathwork practitioners during a single session, with no comparison group, so the findings are preliminary.

“Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood,” Schmitz said.

“Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate.”

Breathing hard and fast for a long time removes carbon dioxide from the blood faster than the body makes it.

Carbon dioxide is one of the main signals that keeps the brain’s small blood vessels open. When it drops, those vessels tighten and less blood gets through.

The team measured blood flow through the brain’s grey matter at the moment each person rated the experience strongest.

At this point, blood flow had fallen from about 30 to about 16 milliliters per 100 grams of tissue per minute. That is a drop of about 45 percent, which is a large change for something a person does on purpose.

Earlier studies have reported signs of the brain not getting enough oxygen when flow falls by 50 to 60 percent. The average here came close to that limit and stayed below it.

A 2025 study of the same kind of intensive breathwork measured a drop of 41.6 percent, and Schmitz’s team wrote that the two results agree.

The 30 volunteers were between 26 and 64 years old, and half were women. Most had practiced intensive breathwork for one to three years, typically less than once a month.

Anyone with a history of a psychiatric or neurological disorder was left out, and so was anyone who had taken a psychedelic in the previous three months.

Each person lay in the scanner and breathed in a continuous circle, with no pause between breaths, for as long as they chose. That ran from about 36 to 96 minutes. Music played the whole time, either their own or the study’s.

Every 12 minutes, the room light came on and the person pressed one of four buttons to rate the experience against the strongest breathwork session of their life.

Medical staff supervised every session, and monitoring continued for at least an hour afterward.

The experiences were strong: on the four-point scale, the average rating at the peak was 3.5, and the most common answer was the top mark.

Within an hour of the session’s end, each person filled in a standard questionnaire on altered states. The profile that came back was dominated by a sense of boundlessness and a drop in alertness, with milder visual changes.

Psychedelics produce a closely similar profile, the authors wrote. The scores were lower, though, than people typically report after a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin.

A person whose blood flow fell the most was no more likely to report an intense experience than a person whose flow fell the least. The size of the drop predicted neither the button ratings during the session nor the questionnaire scores afterward.

One reading, the authors wrote, is that the drop works like a threshold. Once blood flow falls far enough, altered states become possible, and falling further doesn’t deepen them.

The team also looked at the default mode network, a set of brain regions that are active together when a person is resting and thinking about themselves.

Psilocybin and LSD reliably weaken the coordination inside that network, and the team expected intensive breathwork to do the same.

Resting scans before and after the session showed no overall change in how tightly those regions worked together. But the people whose network connections weakened the most reported the most intense altered states.

The team found that link under one way of cleaning the scan data and not under another, so they called it tentative. The drop in blood flow didn’t predict the network change either.

So the authors described two partly separate things: a brain getting far less blood and, in some people, a reorganizing network that goes with the experience itself.

The team presented the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich in October.

Everyone in the study was an experienced practitioner, so how a first-timer’s brain responds is an open question.

The network scans were taken after the breathing stopped, not during it, because the chest and head movement of circular breathing ruins that kind of scan. Any change that faded quickly was missed.

The team didn’t measure carbon dioxide in the breath, and there was no comparison session of plain rest. Music played throughout, which the authors wrote can change the same network on its own.

Hana Adolphi at the Central Institute of Mental Health co-coordinated the study and is a co-author on the publication. “Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness,” she said.

“Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance,” she added.

Whether the network change happens during the breathing itself, rather than after it, is the question this design couldn’t answer.

The authors wrote that future studies need scanning methods that can cope with the motion of hard breathing, and a plain resting session to compare against.

The full study was published in the journal Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry.

#6408. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6407. Curiosity captures a martian dawn

The morning Sun casts a hazy glow over Mars’ Mount Sharp, lighting up distant wind-carved rock formations known as yardangs. This scene is cropped from a six-image panorama captured by the Mastcam on NASA’s Curiosity rover at 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 11, 2026, the mission’s 4,982nd sol (martian day). Mount Sharp, formally Aeolis Mons, stands 3.4 miles (5.5 km) tall at the center of Mars’ 96-mile-wide (154 km) Gale Crater. Since 2014, Curiosity has climbed roughly 0.6 mile (1 km) up its stratified slopes, reading each new layer like a chapter of martian geology.

The mountain’s lowest, oldest layers likely formed from sediment deposited by lakes and streams that have long since vanished. This photo is the most detailed view to date of the much younger yardang layer. Of particular interest is the fact that the color and orientation of the yardangs don’t match the surrounding material. Scientists think these features could have been built up from volcanic ash that settled after a nearby eruption, and was then carved away by the wind. Curiosity should reach the yardangs’ base in 2027, where its instruments will help uncover how the layer formed.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6406. A farmer in Mexico saw the ground split open in his cornfield, then watched a volcano grow to 1,391 feet tall

In 1943, Mexico's Parícutin volcano erupted from a farmer's cornfield, growing rapidly and burying two villages during nine years of activity.

On February 20, 1943, farmer Dionisio Pulido watched a fissure open in his field near the village of Parícutin, in the Mexican state of Michoacán. Smoke rose from the crack, along with a hissing sound and a smell of sulfur.

Within a week, the new cone stood more than 490 feet (150 meters) tall. When the eruption ended in 1952, it had risen 1,391 feet (424 meters) above the cornfield where it began.

Lava buried two villages along the way. Parícutin was the first volcano whose eruption modern scientists observed in detail from its birth, according to the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS).

Starting around February 5 to 7, 1943, local witnesses felt about two weeks of earthquake activity before the eruption.

Felipe Cuara Amezcua, then municipal president of San Juan Parangaricutiro, later reported that the tremors grew until more than 200 shook the area in a single day.

On February 20, Pulido went to his farm to prepare the fields for the spring sowing. He had owned the land for 31 years.

Smithsonian mineralogist William F. Foshag and Mexican geologist Jenaro González R. later collected his account and his wife’s. A 1956 U.S. Geological Survey bulletin printed them in English translation.

At about 4 p.m., Pulido left his wife, Paula, and went to burn a pile of branches. She had been hearing underground noise and thunder.

“About 4 p. m., after talking to my husband, I heard a kind of loud whistle,” Paula Pulido recalled.

“I saw that it was a kind of fissure that had only a depth of half a meter,” Pulido said.

He then saw the ground swell by about 6.6 to 8 feet (2 to 2.5 meters), while gray smoke or dust rose from the crack.

“Immediately more smoke began to rise, with a hiss or whistle, loud and continuous,” he recounted.

Frightened, he mounted his mare and galloped to the village where his family was waiting.

Accounts from Pulido and other witnesses gave “the first adequate account of the birth of a new volcano,” Foshag and González wrote.

One of the first photographs of the eruption, taken at 6 p.m. on February 20, shows an ash plume rising from the new vent. By midnight, the cone was about 20 feet (6 meters) high.

On the morning of February 21, a strong earthquake caused panic. People from Parícutin fled to San Juan Parangaricutiro, and many from San Juan went on to Angahuan or Uruapan.

A photograph from February 21 shows the cone about 100 feet (30 meters) tall, just rising above the treetops. After six days of activity, it reached 548 feet (167 meters).

The first lava flow, called the Quitzocho flow, moved north over cornfields prepared for planting. Mexican geologist Ezequiel Ordóñez estimated that the early lava advanced about 10 feet (3 meters) an hour.

Ash fell too. It piled up deeper than 6 inches (15 centimeters) over an area of 116 square miles (300 square kilometers) around the volcano.

When the first phase of activity ended on October 19, 1943, the original vent had built a cone about 1,200 feet (365 meters) high.

Pulido’s home village lay only 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) northwest of the new cone. Its 733 residents had to abandon it for good four months after the eruption began, and lava later flowed over the site.

Starting in January 1944, a new phase sent out the Taquí lava flows, which spread over about 7 square miles (18 square kilometers) by 1945.

In July 1944, lava surrounded the church of San Juan Parangaricutiro. Its tower still stands in the middle of a lava flow, the IUGS notes.

In all, the volcano’s lavas reached up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) from the vent and formed a field of about 9.7 square miles (25 square kilometers).

The Mexican government gave displaced residents new land in Caltzontzín, 17 miles (27 kilometers) to the southeast.

Parícutin was “the first well-documented example of an eruption of a monogenetic volcanic cone in historical time,” according to a 1993 USGS film report.

A monogenetic cone forms during a single eruptive episode. Parícutin, active for about nine years, gave scientists an unprecedented chance to follow such a volcano through its full life cycle.

An international group documented the activity in real time. Celedonio Gutiérrez, a resident of San Juan who kept a diary from the first day, worked with U.S. scientists throughout the eruption.

In 1990, volcanologists I. Yokoyama and S. de la Cruz-Reyna analyzed the precursory earthquakes of the 1943 eruption, a type of signal that comes before eruptions.

In 1985, decades after the eruption stopped, a fumarole at Parícutin still measured 883°F (473°C). The cone is one of more than 1,400 vents in the Michoacán-Guanajuato volcanic field.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program.

The top pet hair vacuums are designed with powerful suction and superior filtration (plus, they come with special attachments) to capture fine hair, thick fur, and pet dander. Regardless of whether you have a fluffy cat, a long-haired pup, or both, investing in a vacuum specifically made for pets will help you keep messes in check for a tidier home.

Upright and canister vacuums are the strongest options for deep cleaning, but cordless stick vacuums, handheld vacuums, and robot vacuums all aid in daily pet hair control. Units that have tangle-free brush rolls and easy-to-empty dustbins are best for reduced maintenance, and a HEPA filter is essential for clearing out dust and dander that may trigger your allergies.

I researched and hands-on-tested lots of vacuums to find versions that truly pick up pet hair, focusing on features, bin capacity, and filtration. Below are my choices, as well as advice and important pointers to consider before you shop.

I initially considered a range of vacuum styles, from uprights to robots to canisters. Keeping in mind different price points, I chose models that provide an optimal combination of suction strength, versatility, pet-focused features and tools, and value.

I tested the Shark AZ2002 Vertex in a home with two American Shorthair cats, three different floor types, and multiple area rugs.
