#6340. Great Wolf Lodge Coupons for November 2026

Family vacations come in all shapes and sizes, but sometimes, it’s all about the kids. That’s when places like Great Wolf Lodge come in clutch. Between the indoor water parks, arcades, and arts and crafts, they’re designed for keeping bundles of energy entertained…both kids and kids at heart. I’ve been to a Great Wolf Lodge once (in LaGrange, just outside of Atlanta) and had a ball going down those water slides and playing arcade games, even as a kid-free twenty-something.

The family resort chain has more than 20 properties across North America; most are clustered on the East Coast and in the Midwest, though there are a handful out west too. If a family vacation calls and you’re looking for ways to save on the stay, keep reading.

Families squeezing in one more vacation before the holidays or planning ahead for next year can use a Great Wolf Lodge promo code to save on stays. Combine your lodging discount with water park passes (included with every stay) for maximum value, and check for seasonal Great Wolf Lodge deals that may include dining credits or attraction passes as well as room savings.

If you're ready to book this week—specifically, by November 8—and are taking a trip through February 25, 2027, you can get up to 50% off select dates. Of note, length of stay requirements may apply, and the offer is valid on standard suites styles (with varied promos on themed and premium suites); there's a limited number of rooms available for each date. Head here to book.

While last-minute discounts do exist, it also pays to plan ahead. Save up to 50% when you book your stay at least 60 days in advance with the Great Wolf Lodge promo code ESAVER. The longer you stay, the more you’ll save—and Great Wolf recently upped the ante with 30% off one-night stays, 40% off two-night stays, and 50% for three-plus night stays. This offer is ideal for guests looking for a Great Wolf Lodge promo code while planning for fall or winter vacations. Of notes, this offer may not be valid during holiday and blackout periods, and cannot be combined with any other discount or promotional offers.

For more short-term plans, use Great Wolf Lodge’s discount code TRIPLEFUN to take up to 40% off your total stay when staying three nights or longer within 60 days of booking. Of note, Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from the deal.

If you’re planning a weekend trip (or a shorter mid-week trip!), use promo code MOREFUN to save 30% on two-night bookings for stays within 60 days of purchase. Again, this code is good for the rest of the year, so keep it tucked in the back of your mind if you’ve got a later-in-the-year trip brewing.

Special discounted rates on Great Wolf Lodge day passes are available for military members (active, retired, and veteran), teachers, fire and emergency medical service personnel, medical providers, nurses, 911 dispatchers, police, government employees, and correctional officers looking for a respite. If you work in one of these professions, use the Great Wolf Lodge discount code WPHEROES to access reduced pricing on stays. This code is good through the end of 2028, and you’ll need to verify your status using ID.me.

Grandparents and older parents can get in on the fun with exclusive savings for guests aged 65 and older when using the promo code SENIORS. Members of AAA, AARP, or other vehicle clubs can also save on lodge bookings. Enter your membership details to activate the Great Wolf Lodge AAA discount or Great Wolf Lodge AARP discount. Points are not earned on any alcohol purchases, taxes, gratuities, fees, or on-site purchases not charged to the suite. You can check your points balance at any time in your Great Wolf profile, and redeem them by booking directly on greatwolf.com while logged into your account.

If all looks good, check the details of the promo code to ensure it's still active and hasn't expired. Some discount codes exclude certain locations, so make sure your booking meets any necessary criteria to qualify. One of my favorite things about World of Hyatt points is how much flexibility they offer. You could redeem just a few thousand points for a night at a Category 1 Hyatt hotel or use a larger stash to book a higher-category hotel or all-inclusive resort.

Since Hyatt still uses award charts for most of its properties, you can sometimes get outsize value by redeeming points when cash rates are high. But free nights aren't the only way to use your points. From room upgrades and dining experiences to airline miles and rental cars, here's how you can redeem World of Hyatt points, including which options offer the best value.

The best way to redeem Hyatt points is usually for free hotel nights. Hyatt has award charts for most free night awards, though some are dynamically priced. There are also ways to combine points with cash and free night certificates.

Hyatt publishes award charts for free night awards at Hyatt hotels and resorts, participating resorts within the Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts. Each of these charts has five award pricing tiers — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper and Top — for each category.

Here's the award chart for standard room award nights at Hyatt hotels and resorts.

Hyatt publishes separate award charts for Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts, as well as for club rooms, standard suites and premium suites. Check out our guide to the Hyatt award charts for all the charts.

You can click on "Points Calendar" on the results page for any particular property when searching for award stays to see how many points each night costs.

However, free night awards at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels and Homes & Hideaways by World of Hyatt are priced dynamically based on paid rates. For example, this night at a Homes & Hideaways property in Florida would cost 16,011 points or $192.13. This means you'd get 1.2 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

And this night at a Mr & Mrs Smith property in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, would cost 8,750 points or $58.91. This means you'd only get 0.67 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each. As such, you'll generally want to get at least this much value when redeeming your Hyatt points.

Related: Best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

You can also book Points + Cash rates for some stays. When these rates are available for your chosen room type and property, you'll redeem 50% of the points required for a free night and get 50% to 70% off the standard rate (which may be higher than the best available rate).

For example, I could redeem 12,000 points, book a Points + Cash rate of 6,000 points plus $156.50 or book a paid rate of $220.16 for this night at the Hyatt Centric Rittenhouse Square Philadelphia.

When redeeming points, I'd get 1.83 cents per point. And when booking a Points + Cash rate, I'd get 1.06 cents per point.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

You can also combine Hyatt points with paid nights and even free night certificates when booking with the Hyatt Pay My Way feature. To use this feature, sign in to your Hyatt account, search for a paid stay, click on the property and room type of your choice and then click on rates until you see one with a Pay My Way option.

Click on the Pay My Way box, and then you can choose whether to use points, cash, Points + Cash or free night certificates for each night.

I often use Pay My Way when redeeming free night certificates, as this lets me book a multinight stay even if I only have one free night certificate. I've also used Pay My Way to redeem points for a stay with one particularly expensive night.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

You can redeem points to upgrade eligible paid stays at many Hyatt hotels and resorts. Here's a look at the upgrade rate per night:

You can sometimes redeem points for an upgrade at the time of booking. In the following example, you could redeem 9,500 points for a premium suite free night, 4,750 points plus $158 for a premium suite Points + Cash booking or 9,000 points plus $152 to upgrade a paid night to a premium suite.

If you don't upgrade at the time of booking, you can call (800) 544-9288 in the U.S. and Canada or contact a Global Care Center to see if your existing stay is eligible for an upgrade with points.

Related: Your ultimate guide to Hyatt hotel brands

You can redeem Hyatt points for dining and spa experiences at participating locations even if you aren't spending the night. Plus, you can redeem points during stays at participating locations to pay for in-room movies, parking, transportation and more.

To redeem points, simply request to use Hyatt points at checkout and choose how many points to redeem. You should be able to redeem points at participating locations based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate you'll get ranges from 1 to 1.54 cents per point, which is below TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.65 cents per point for Hyatt points. As such, you'll usually want to find higher-value ways to redeem your Hyatt points.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Find experiences. For example, you could pay $60 plus taxes or redeem 4,286 points for this one-hour aerial yoga and meditation class.

Or, you could redeem 5,357 points or pay $75 plus taxes for an e-bike tour of San Diego.

It's worth taking a look at Find experiences, especially if you select Find experience credits as Hyatt Milestone Rewards. But you usually won't get outsize value when redeeming points for these experiences.

Related: Why bidding on a Hyatt Find experience auction might be the most valuable way to redeem your World of Hyatt points

You can convert Hyatt points into airline miles with the following programs:

For most of the airline programs, you'll get 1 mile for every 2.5 Hyatt points you convert. However, Hyatt uses different conversion rates for Aeromexico Rewards, Air China PhoenixMiles, China Eastern Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Southwest Rapid Rewards and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

You must convert at least 5,000 points at a time but can convert additional points in increments of 1,250. If you convert 50,000 points or more, you'll usually get an extra 5,000 bonus miles.

However, converting Hyatt points to airline miles will rarely make sense. Conversions can take six to eight weeks. Plus, at the usual 2.5:1 conversion ratio, transferring 5,000 Hyatt points yields 2,000 airline miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd be giving up approximately $82.50 in Hyatt points for those 2,000 miles.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Avis free day awards, which are valid at participating locations in the U.S. and Canada, by calling (800) 544-9288. When available, you can redeem 6,000 points per day for an intermediate-size car. However, there are blackout periods that you'll see on the redemption certificate once you redeem your points. Avis free day awards usually expire one year after they're issued.

World of Hyatt members can redeem points for an Aeroplan flight reward certificate valid on Air Canada flights. The 30,000-point certificate costs 50,000 Hyatt points, and you can apply it toward the base fare in points of an Aeroplan flight reward.

Given that TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each and Aeroplan points at 1.45 cents each, this won't be a good-value redemption for most travelers. However, if you were planning to convert Hyatt points to Aeroplan points, the flight reward certificate might provide better value.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

World of Hyatt and American Airlines AAdvantage are winding down their partnership. But eligible Explorist and Globalist members can redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day until 1 a.m. EST on Nov. 16.

You can redeem 5,000 Hyatt points to get AAdvantage Gold status for a day, 8,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum status for a day and 12,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum Pro status for a day.

However, you can only use these awards on your own travel itineraries, and some fares aren't eligible.

Related: Why I rely on credit cards to earn American Airlines elite status

Finally, you can redeem Hyatt points for a future meeting credit to use for meetings and catered events at participating Hyatt hotels and resorts based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate is 1.33 cents per point regardless of how many points you redeem toward a future meeting credit. You must call a Hyatt Global Care Center to redeem points for a future meeting credit. You can't use future meeting credits at Hyatt Vacation Club, Bahia Principe and Destination by Hyatt Residences locations.

Redeeming World of Hyatt points for free nights is usually the best way to get good value from your points. I particularly like redeeming Hyatt points at hotels where cash rates are high, as I can often get outsize value. But I'll also redeem points on stays with resort fees, as Hyatt waives resort fees on free night awards.

Other redemption options, including room upgrades, Find experiences and airline miles, can make sense in certain situations. But I generally recommend saving your Hyatt points for free night awards, especially if you can be flexible about where and when you stay.

#6337. The Best Hot Dogs in Chicago, According to Someone Who Has Tried 'Em All

If you’re looking for the best hot dog in Chicago, you’ve come to the right place. While I can’t tell you how many hot dogs I’ve eaten in my life, I am sure that number is in the many thousands. After high school, I worked at Nick’s Nest, a hot dog stand in my Massachusetts hometown, where I would have one for lunch every day. They’re a favorite food to eat while traveling, and I regularly grab them in my daily life as well, because I live in Chicago, where the hot dog is a local staple.

Served in a steamed poppyseed bun, the Chicago dog has specific toppings: mustard, chopped onions, neon green relish, tomatoes (slices or wedges), pickles (usually spears, sometimes chips), spicy sport peppers, and celery salt. The all-beef dog has a natural casing, which gives a perfect snap when you bite into it. While most Chicago dogs are pretty good, the best ones are constructed so you taste everything in every bite. And you probably know this, but just to be sure: that bite will not include ketchup, as the tangy condiment doesn’t mesh with the other toppings (this is a real if-you-know-you-know thing in Chicago—and you want to be in the know). When you’re in the city, whether you’re siddling up to a hot dog stand or popping into a casual restaurant, order yours as a “Chicago dog” or ask for it “dragged through the garden”—a signal that you know what’s up, and that you want everything on it.

These are the best places to get a hot dog in Chicago, according to a dog-loving resident.

Read our complete Chicago travel guide here, which includes:

It feels very Chicago that you can get an excellent hot dog inside Home Depot. Fixin’ Franks is a family-owned spot with outposts in stores around the city. You’ll find the stands tucked near the exit, where it’s a treat for finishing all your home-repair shopping. There’s a tight, locally sourced menu of hot dogs, Polish and Maxwell Street sausages, Italian beef, and elotes. Get a classic Chicago dog—and if you want to push the envelope, add J.P. Graziano hot giardiniera on top.

1017 W. Irving Park Rd., Lakeview; 1701 W. Lawrence Ave., Ravenswood

While most restaurants follow the dragged-through-the-garden approach, Byron’s, which served their hot dogs at the White House during the Obama administration, takes a different approach. The standard dressing at the 51-year-old stand consists of mustard, relish, onions, tomato, pickle spears, and celery salt, and adds lettuce, green peppers, and cucumber slices (hot peppers are available on request). While this is, admittedly, a lot to maneuver while eating, the salad approach adds a lot of freshness and almost makes it seem like a healthy choice.

1250 S. Union Ave., University Village; 2775 N. Elston Ave., Avondale

Must order: Polish sausage sandwich, pork chop sandwich

Chicago’s hot dog stand culture includes more than just dogs. Jim’s is the best place for two other local beloveds: The Maxwell Street Polish and the pork chop sandwich. The Polish, a garlicky smoked beef and pork link, is generally credited to the stand’s namesake, Macedonian immigrant Jimmy Stefanovic, who took over his aunt and uncle’s stand in 1939. It’s served with mustard, tons of grilled onions, and sport peppers. The pork chop sandwich, served bone-in (bite carefully!) comes with the same garnishes, as does the all-beef hot dog. There’s no seating at the University Village location, which is open from 6 a.m. to 1 a.m., but you can eat at the metal counter or sit on the curb—Jim’s always feels like a party.

Must order: Hot dog, chocolate cake shake

When visitors come to town and want to try Chicago classics, I send them to Portillo’s. The local chain, which Dick Portillo founded in 1963, offers solid versions of local favorites, including hot dogs, Italian beef, and a Maxwell Street Polish. The steamed dog is expertly done and a go-to. Also a go-to is the chocolate cake shake, which is made with—you guessed it—a slice of chocolate cake blitzed into a milkshake. It’s decadently rich, and a true Chicago experience.

3057 N. Ashland Ave., Lakeview; 2449 W. Armitage Ave., Logan Square; 500 W. 35th St., Bridgeport; 4811 Dempster St., Skokie

Must-order: Hot dog and fries, RHR double cheeseburger

With four locations of this locally beloved stand (the O.G. Bridgeport location goes by 35th Street Red Hots), you are never far from one of the city’s best dogs. The links are served Depression-style, which means they have stripped-down toppings: just mustard, onion, relish, and sport peppers, with a pile of fries on top, for a full meal that tops out at just $5.20. Many locals, myself included, feel that Red Hot Ranch’s double smashburger is the best in the city, so get one of those to split as well.

6363 N. Milwaukee Ave., Norwood Park East; 333 S. Milwaukee Ave., Wheeling

In 1948, Maurie and Flaurie Berman opened their drive-in with two signatures. First, the couple appears as 12-foot hot dog statues on the building’s roof—you can’t miss this duo. And second, they serve a hot dog with a point of view: It’s a custom all-beef dog a bit larger than your standard link, and topped with mustard,

a pickle, sport peppers, and chopped onions, plus piccalilli and a pickled green tomato. It comes tucked with crinkle-cut fries in a custom cardboard box, which you can even peep in an episode of The Bear.

Must-order: Chicago-style Duck Inn Dog, fried cheese curds

What happens when you take a Chicago classic and put it in the hands of one of the city’s best chefs? You get Kevin Hickey’s Duck Inn Dog. Every element is made to Hickey’s specs: The juicy beef, pork, and duck fat sausage is grilled, tucked in a brioche poppyseed bun, and dressed with a “supercondiment” of mustard and relish mixed with tomato and onion. It’s finished with a dill pickle, pickled serranos, and celery salt (and perfect with fried cheese curds alongside). This is the glow-up the humble dog deserves.

Much of the love for 43-year-old The Wiener’s Circle is for its heckling servers, led by local institution Poochie Rollins. That experience is one reason to visit the Lincoln Park stand, which is famously open until 4 a.m. on weekends (and 2 a.m. the rest of the week). The other? The excellent food, like the char dog. Most stands steam their dogs, but the charring approach here adds a smoky flavor and crisper texture. Do not miss the fantastic cheese fries, with a generous dollop of tangy cheddar sauce.

Most hot dog stands in Chicago use locally made Vienna Beef links, and it’s worth venturing straight to the source to try one at this cafe, which is located across the street from the factory. Snag a red stool and order the textbook Chicago-style dog and a side of crispy fries. After lunch, peruse the goodies in the shop, which range from cases of hot dogs to hot dog stuffies.

Artur Wnorowski’s casual Polish joint serves some of my favorite sausages in town. All are made in-house: The kielbasa, which he learned to make from his grandfather, is smoked over pecan wood and dressed with caramelized onions, sport peppers, and hazy IPA mustard, while the all-beef dog is available Chicago-style or Polish-inspired. With sauerkraut, onions, sour cream, and a potato and cheese pierogi on top, it’s a nod to the sense of fun Chicago’s hot dog stands deliver.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

With more than 9,000 properties across over 35 brands worldwide, Marriott Bonvoy offers plenty of ways to earn free hotel stays.

Whether you're looking for a premium travel card, a no-annual-fee option or a business card, Marriott's cobranded credit card lineup has something to offer.

Below, we break down the current offers and help you decide which Marriott card might be worth it.

Marriott Bonvoy loyalists can choose from card options issued by American Express and Chase.

There are multiple personal cards and one business card available. Make sure you’re eligible for a business card before applying. Keep in mind that TPG recommends a credit score in the good-to-excellent range to give yourself the best possible chance of approval.

*The bonus value is based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Marriott stays?

Best for: Travelers who only stay with Marriott once or twice each year

The is one of Chase’s two mid-tier Bonvoy cards.

Welcome offer: Earn three free night awards (valued up to 50,000 points each) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. Additionally, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

Per our valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,225 (including the statement credit).

We recommend applying when at least 150,000 points are on offer, making now a great time to apply.

Why we like it: The Boundless gives you great Marriott perks without paying a high annual fee. With this card, you’ll get automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and 15 elite qualifying nights every year. You’ll also earn one elite night credit toward the next level of elite status for every $5,000 spent, and you can reach Gold Elite status by spending $35,000 on the card in a calendar year.

The card's most valuable perk is the annual free night award (worth up to 35,000 points) at each account anniversary, though Marriott’s lack of award charts could hinder your ability to use this benefit.

Fortunately, this free night award can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless card.

Best for: Small-business owners who can maximize the card's annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees)

The is Marriott’s only business card currently available to new applicants.

Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, this bonus is worth up to $563.

This is the standard offer, so it's worth waiting for an elevated bonus.

Why we like it: With this card, you’ll get automatic Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and a 7% discount on eligible bookings made directly with Marriott through an eligible channel at participating properties with this card’s rate.

The card also comes with 15 elite night credits annually (which can be stacked with a Marriott Bonvoy consumer card) and a free night award annually after your card renewal month (worth up to 35,000 points and can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night). In addition, you can earn a second free night (also worth up to 35,000 points) after $60,000 of purchases on your card in a calendar year. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

Marriott’s use of dynamic pricing may make it hard to use these awards. Still, you should be able to find a participating property that can cover your annual fee (and then some), as our data indicates there’s still significant value in the program.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Business.

Best for: Mega Marriott fans who stay with the brand at least a few times each year

Welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $750.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: The card also has valuable perks, such as automatic Platinum Elite status, an annual free night award (worth up to 85,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees) after card renewal month, up to $300 per year (up to $25 in monthly statement credits) for eligible purchases at restaurants worldwide, Priority Pass™ lounge access and 25 elite qualifying night credits per year. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Remember that Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so you may need to work harder to find a property where you can use your free nights. But you can top up free night awards with up to 25,000 points now, which allows you to book a night worth up to 110,000 points.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant.

The is Bonvoy’s mid-tier card from American Express. It has earnings, benefits and an annual fee that mirror the Bountiful.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

This bonus is worth $638, per TPG's valuations.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: This card also offers mid-tier perks, including complimentary Gold Elite status, a solid earning rate at Marriott properties and elite night credits. However, it lacks several benefits that you might expect from a mid-tier card.

For example, you must spend $15,000 in a calendar year to earn a free night (worth up to 50,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees). Other Marriott cards with lower annual fees offer a similar perk with no spending requirement, making this card tough to justify keeping after earning the welcome offer in the first year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Bevy.

Best for: High-spending Marriott fans who prefer to bank with Chase

The Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful is the other mid-tier Bonvoy card from Chase.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $638.

This is typically the standard welcome offer we see in the card's history. Unless you absolutely need this card now, you’re better off applying when the offer is higher.

Why we like it: While American Express issues the Bevy, the Bountiful comes from Chase. The two cards offer mostly the same benefits, making it hard to justify the Bountiful's $250 annual fee. However, the welcome bonus may interest you.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card.

Best for: Travelers who infrequently stay with Marriott, but want to enjoy perks when they do

The is Chase’s entry-level card for Bonvoy enthusiasts.

Welcome offer: Earn 45,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The bonus points are worth $338, according to TPG’s valuations.

This is slightly higher than the standard welcome offer we've seen on the card, but we'd still suggest waiting for a more rewarding bonus if your timeline is flexible.

Why we like it: The card offers automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and five annual elite night credits. It also charges no foreign transaction fees. Additionally, the Bold features Chase’s Pay Yourself Back, allowing you to redeem points toward eligible travel purchases made directly with airlines or Marriott Bonvoy hotels (up to $750 in total redemptions per year).

This is a solid set of perks for a card with no annual fee. However, frequent Marriott guests may do better with a card that offers more perks during each stay.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bold card.

If multiple Marriott card offers intrigue you, you can indeed have more than one Marriott card open. Some TPG staffers have two or three.

It can make sense to leverage the annual anniversary award nights and stack the 5 to 25 elite nights awarded by carrying both a personal and a small-business Marriott card.

However, with six Marriott cards available to new applicants, there are several restrictions on who can earn the welcome offers across the cards, especially since Marriott cards are issued by both Amex and Chase.

Note that these restrictions are all in addition to Chase’s 5/24 rule (which applies to new applicants for the Bold, Boundless and Bountiful cards) and Amex’s one-bonus-per-lifetime rule (which applies to the Bevy, Brilliant and Business cards).

Make sure you’re eligible for these offers before applying.

Related: Here’s how to calculate your Chase 5/24 standing

Marriott credit cards regularly rank among the best hotel credit cards thanks to the long-term value they offer through perks such as elite status and annual free night awards.

The Boundless currently has a great welcome offer; we'd recommend holding off for higher bonuses on the other cards.

Before applying, consider the size of the welcome offer, whether you're eligible and if the card's ongoing benefits justify adding it to your wallet.

#6335. This Train Offers a Front-Row Seat to One of Colorado’s Greatest Natural Wonders

“Locomotives all have their own attitudes and personalities,” says Adam Clawson, the 24-year-old engineer at the helm of Royal Gorge Route Railroad, as our train winds along the Arkansas River. “They are their own living, breathing machines, and you have to learn their personalities.”

It’s a warm Saturday afternoon in October, and Clawson is at the controls of a locomotive he knows well: “Black Betty,” a jet-black, 3,000-horsepower diesel-electric unit that runs along a 12-mile stretch of tracks in Southern Colorado. Clawson is a third-generation railroader, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and great-grandfather, who both worked along this same route.

The Royal Gorge Route Railroad winds along the Arkansas River in Colorado.

As he eases the rumbling locomotive through the gorge, he offers a running commentary on the geology and history unfolding outside the window. Millions of years ago, he says, as the Rockies rose above the plains, the Arkansas River began carving its ancient path through the emerging peaks. Over time, the water wore away the hard granite, cutting a narrow, V-shaped gorge that plunges as deep as 1,250 feet in places.

The result is the Royal Gorge, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls.

The writer's view aboard the Royal Gorge Route Railroad

This train line is as historic as it is scenic. Though the tourist train didn't launch until 1998, the route itself has been here for nearly 150 years—but it was close to never being built in the first place. In the late 1870s, a pair of competing railroad companies—the Denver & Rio Grande and the Santa Fe—duked it out for the chance to build tracks through this narrow canyon. Their two-year battle, which involved everything from court injunctions to sabotage to gun-slinging hired guards, became known as the “Royal Gorge War.” Eventually, the two companies signed a treaty and the Denver & Rio Grande prevailed, building tracks that eventually reached the lucrative mining hub of Leadville.

Decades later, the train still threads through the same Old West landscape, but the ride is decidedly more comfortable. Today passengers can choose from three classes: Vista Dome, which offers nearly unobstructed views of the gorge from glass-enclosed dome cars; Deluxe Class in the vintage dining car, where four-top tables with cushioned booth-style seats and a bar are nestled against the large windows; and Coach Class, with four-person table seating and the option to order food and drink from the casual grill menu and bar. On select dates, there are also First Class dining tickets available for lunch and dinner, with elevated menus and wine pairings. Regardless of where you sit, all ticket holders have access to the open-air car, which is standing-room only. With Clawson or one of his fellow engineers at the controls, all travelers have to do is sit back and let the scenery unfold.

The journey begins roughly an hour south of Colorado Springs in Cañon City at a historic depot originally completed in 1914. A few miles later, a dilapidated pipeline comes into view, running along the canyon wall just above the river. Completed in 1910, this eight-mile-long, mostly wooden structure provided water to Cañon City until 1973. As the train passes under the Royal Gorge Bridge, Clawson encourages me to open the cab window, lean back, and look up. The wind whips my hair as I stare at the bridge some 1,000 feet overhead. It’s 18 feet wide, according to Clawson, but from this vantage point, it looks like a thin wire that’s been strung across a gaping expanse.

As the train works its way through the river gorge, water rushes past and red rock walls tower on both sides.

Next, the train squeezes through the gorge’s narrowest and deepest section, the towering red granite walls growing taller and more imposing as they tighten around the tracks. Then we chug over the famous “Hanging Bridge,” which was an engineering marvel when it was completed in 1879—and remains one even today. At this point, the chasm narrows to just 30 feet wide, creating a bottleneck that required a little ingenuity to get a train through. Engineer C. Shallor Smith came up with a brilliant solution: He designed a 175-foot-long bridge that’s suspended above the rushing water by A-shaped supports anchored to the canyon wall.

Soon after, Clawson spots a pair of plastic kayaks hauled out on a small beach on the other side of the waterway. “We might get mooned,” he warns, referencing how paddlers traditionally greet the train when it passes. But when we spot the kayakers standing on the bank a few minutes later, they simply smile and wave. Clawson blares the train’s horn in response.

Eventually, the train reaches its western terminus, the town of Parkdale. Clawson hits the brakes and we jump down onto the tracks. Standing in front of the train up close, I’m struck by just how imposing she is. Thinking back to Clawson’s personality comment, I imagine her as fiercely independent—a self-assured, no-nonsense type of gal who’s not easily pushed around.

We clamber back into the cab and the train heads in reverse, retracing the route toward Cañon City. I relax back into my seat, letting the engine’s vibrations and the rhythmic drone of the wheels lull me into a pleasant daze. Outside, the rocky surfaces of the gorge’s walls alternate between light and shadow while the river glints in the midday sun. High overhead, I spot a turkey vulture circling on a thermal, its wings arching in a shallow V as it glides without flapping.

Clawson follows my gaze. “You can’t make this up,” he says. “Somebody might type into AI, ‘Take this picture of me and make it look like I’m in paradise.’ [But] all I gotta do is step outside."

#6333. 10 Magical Christmas Traditions Around the World

Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers—although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else.

Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season.

Christmas is not recognized as a national holiday in Japan, but the festive season is still celebrated—albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken—a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too—strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite.

As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes—mostly fish-based—served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of January 5, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious.

The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s—or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place—the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer.

While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race."

Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces—in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveler US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70s Fahrenheit with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)."

While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette.

In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier."

Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child, my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew—an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition."

Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents—in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre, or downright useless objects instead.

"For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting."

Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip—sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties.

"In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

#6331. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. #6330. Air Serbia Flight To Nowhere: A320 Forced To Return To Belgrade Over Mysterious Security Concern

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and returning to Belgrade over a security concern involving one passenger. Serbian media identified that passenger as the country’s former intelligence chief, who allegedly boarded without completing security screening. He denies wrongdoing.

As flagged by One Mile At A Time, Air Serbia flight JU134 departed Belgrade for Moscow on November 3, 2026, but turned back over southern Lithuania. According to Serbian media, the Airbus A320 left at 6:48 PM and returned shortly before 10:00 PM. Passengers spent more than three hours flying only to end up where they started.

Air Serbia confirmed that airport authorities requested additional security checks concerning one passenger. The airline said it returned in accordance with the instructions it received, but did not publicly identify that passenger.

The passenger in question has since been identified as Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia’s former intelligence chief. It appears that someone helped him board without completing the required screening and that the airport’s corporate security director ordered the return after reviewing surveillance footage.

Vulin insists he completed the required checks, was carrying no prohibited items, and was being targeted for political reasons (his pro-Russian party lost in a snap election last month). He said his trip concerned negotiations over Serbia’s gas arrangement with Russia.

Passengers and their luggage underwent additional screening in Belgrade. The flight eventually continued to Moscow with a replacement crew, arriving about seven hours late.

If the reports are accurate, the obvious question is how someone was allowed to board without completing the required checks. Political prominence should not provide an exemption from an aviation security procedure, though I understand how easy it is to open an employee access door for a VIP).

But Vulin disputes that account, and the airline’s statement establishes only that authorities requested additional screening. That leaves important questions about what happened before departure and what prompted the return. Vulin was allowed to continue on the delayed flight to Moscow.

Belgrade’s Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has requested an investigation into the circumstances, including whether procedures were followed, who authorized the aircraft’s return, and what security assessment supported that decision.

That inquiry is appropriate. If someone bypassed screening, there should be accountability for how it happened. If the checks were properly completed, authorities need to explain why an aircraft full of passengers was brought back.

This is all may be Serbian domestic politics…

An alleged screening lapse involving a former intelligence chief turned a routine Air Serbia flight into a lengthy journey back to its starting point. The aircraft eventually reached Moscow, but the competing accounts of what happened remain unresolved.

I hope the investigation establishes whether someone received preferential treatment or whether there is another explanation for this extraordinary return. Either way, the passengers arrived very late into Moscow.

#6329. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6328. The 50 Best Restaurants For 2026 Have Been Announced—With a Remote European Spot in First Place

The 50 Best Restaurants for 2026 have just been announced as part of a prestigious awards ceremony in Lima on Wednesday, November 5, 2026. As with every year, we wait for the release—an indicator of which restaurants will be topping travelers' lists in the year ahead, and the trends that will shape the experiences they offer. Below, we cover which restaurant snagged the top spot, which restaurant led on every continent, and the industry stars celebrated with individual awards like Best Pastry Chef, Best Sommelier, and more.

Read on for the full list, and notable takeaways from the winners. (For more on the trends revealed at the Lima event, read our reporter's conversation with winning chefs here.)

The Best Restaurant in the World for 2026 is hidden away in sleepy Basque village, Axpe.

Climbing up from its number two spot in last year's list, this year’s winner is Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, in Spain's Basque Country.

Basque wood-fired cooking is at the heart of this rustic fine-dining restaurant. Chef-owner Víctor Arguinzoniz (also known as Bittor Arginzoniz) is considered a pioneer of grilling and live-fire cooking. At Asador Etxebarri, every course of Bittor Arginzoniz's €300 euro (about $337 USD) tasting menu touches the wood and charcoal grills—from Palamós red prawns to smoked milk ice cream.

Hidden away in the sleepy mountain village of Axpe, about 45 minutes by car from Bilbao, foodies have been making the pilgrimage to try Arguinzoniz's signature grilled dishes since the restaurant opened in 1990. It's been an 18-year journey to the top, as Asador Etxebarri has been a mainstay on The World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2008, starting at number 44.

Once a restaurant gets the coveted number-one trophy, it is ineligible for nomination in forthcoming years—with the intention of allowing other restaurants a chance to earn top billing. Top-placing restaurants are then inducted into a new list, called the Best of the Best. This list includes such legendary eateries as Chef Thomas Keller's The French Laundry in Yountville, California, and Disfrutar in Barcelona, Spain. Last year’s winner, Maido in Lima, Peru, is the most recent inductee to this prestigious list.

It’s tempting to imagine the enviable job held by a panel of judges that sample every restaurant in the world. But that’s not quite how the 50 Best works. Rather, the 50 is an international media company that taps the expertise of over a thousand hospitality experts from around the world to weigh in on the industry that they know best. Chefs, restaurateurs, food journalists, and well-traveled gourmets all anonymously nominate restaurants that they have dined at within the last 18 months. (Members can’t vote for a restaurant they have a financial interest in.) Professional services consultancy Deloitte has access to the voting data to ensure the validity and fairness of the process.

Because of the voting-style nature of the awards, a restaurant might fall off the list one year only to return later. This year, previous entries to the list such as The Ledbury—a fine-dining beauty in London, United Kingdom where chef Brett Graham marries British produce, Japanese flavours, and French culinary techniques—returns to the list in the number 83 spot. Similarly, Luxe Mosu in Seoul, South Korea—home to chef Sung Anh's elevated interpretations of traditional Korean fare—returns to the list at number 78.

“Every year The 50 Best Restaurants list gives us a snapshot of where more than 1,100 individuals who live and breathe this industry have had their most memorable restaurant experiences over the previous 18 months," explains Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50. “And I think that’s what makes it so special. Each Academy member votes independently, so nobody at The 50 or any of our partners has a say in who makes the list, and restaurants can’t nominate themselves. This means every restaurant on the list has genuinely earned it.”

Gaggan in Bangkok climbed up to Number 2 after placing at Number 6 the year prior.

As always, the highest-ranking restaurants on each continent have been given a special mention during tonight's awards—and there are a few repeats from last year. Gaggan in Bangkok (this year's number 2) won the best restaurant in Asia again. Mexico City's Quintonil (4) was the best restaurant in Latin America again, while New York City's Atomix (11) was the best restaurant in North America. Dubai's Trèsind Studio (28) was named the best restaurant in the Middle East for another year. The best restaurant in Africa was Cape Town's La Colombe (35). Sydney's Saint Peter (50) was the best restaurant in Oceania, while top spot Asador Etxebarri took the best restaurant in Europe award.

Every year, the panel awards special prizes to chefs, front-of-house staff, and activists who are leading the charge in hospitality. In 2026, the Best Female Chef Award went to Jessica Rosval, head chef of Al Gatto Verde. Bangkok’s Dej Kewkacha won Best Pastry Chef Award, and Lesley Liu of Odette in Singapore won the Best Sommelier Award while the Estrella Damm Chefs' Choice Award went to Junghyun ‘JP’ Park from Atomix in New York City. Doris Lam won The 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship. Spanish chef Ferran Adrià of El Bulli won the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Restaurants given a special mention during the 2026 ceremony included Tuju in São Paulo, which earned the Highest New Entry Award. Copenhagen's Kadeau won the Highest Climber Award after soaring 33 places this year, and Naar in Kasauli, India, won the Sustainable Restaurant Award.

This year, only one US restaurant made the top 50: Atomix, in New York. It came in 11th place, rising one place from 2025, when it ranked 12.

#6327. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6326. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

Laura Burns is a frequent traveller with an affinity for fine coffee, delicious food and the world's most beautiful sights. If she's writing about it, it's worth exploring. Happiest in Tokyo, Melbourne,... More by Laura Burns

#6325. The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs

On November 4, Lima, Peru, was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri, which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week.

In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here.

Lobster from Kjolle in Lima, which was just named No.7 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list.

Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler. “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.”

It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.”

Saint Peter in Sydney came in at No. 50 on the list, and was named the Best Restaurant in Oceania.

At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen—number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year.

La Colombe in Cape Town debuted a Secret Cellar in 2024, an intimate subterranean enclave where guests hand over their phones before the meal begins. While chef James Gaag understands that some people want to take photos of their food—and certainly that Instagram traffic helps restaurants—he hopes for, but isn't counting on, more phone-free restaurant experiences.

So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.”

Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time.

The Sardine Pie at New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen, which placed number eight on the list.

Kadeau was also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June.

Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed with tweezers; narrative-driven tasting menus that span six or seven hours. These used to scream luxury. Now? Simplicity speaks louder. It’s a trend noted by executive chef James Gaag of La Colombe in the Constantia Valley near Cape Town, owned by chef-proprietor Scot Kirton. La Colombe landed at number 35 and also took home the title of Best Restaurant in Africa.

La Colombe in South Africa placed No. 35 on the list.

At La Colombe and elsewhere, Gaag is energized by “less courses, fresher courses, lighter courses, less time at the table.” His innovative menus might be inspired by both his German upbringing and world travels, but that doesn’t mean trying to fit the entire globe in one menu. “We used to put 100 ingredients on each plate, and I think the longer I run the restaurant, the more confident I am in putting less on the plate,” he continued.

Chef Jeremy Chan, who owns Michelin-starred Ikoyi in London with co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, continues to rise. Ikoyi landed at number 48 this year, owing to its contemporary global menu that is inspired by both British microseasonality and meticulously sourced global spices. For Chan, though, fine dining doesn’t mean frigid. “Fine dining is about creating a refined experience, rather than a sense of preciousness or formality,” he told Condé Nast Traveler. “For me, it is about the refinement and technique of the craft, alongside the responsibility and precision in what we do to make people feel special.”

Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Royer, placed at number 15 this year—one of the many high-ranking spots across Asia, including Gaggan in Bangkok (number 2, and also the Best Restaurant in Asia), Wing in Hong Kong (number 5), and the Chairman (number 6), also in Hong Kong. Condé Nast Traveler asked Chef de Cuisine Sheng Xiong—who blends his Asian heritage with French training for Odette’s menus—if there’s a fine dining trend he’d be happy to see vanish. “You mean we’re going to lose our jobs?” He joked. After his laughter subsided, the chef at the Three Michelin-starred restaurant echoed Chan’s sentiments: “I think moving forward, maybe the white-glove service [will go], because in our restaurant we treat everyone coming in like [they are] coming back home as a family member. It can be a bit too casual sometimes, and at the same time, it makes them feel comfortable. Guests are happy. At the start, Singaporeans, the older generation couldn't understand what we are doing, but as time goes by, they actually prefer that to a very stiff kind of environment.”

A Bluefin Tuna Rhubarb dish at London's Ikoyi, which landed at No. 48 on the list this year.

Chef Niko Romito of the lauded, three Michelin-starred Reale—which placed at number 27 this year—is seeing a difference in the way travelers experience his restaurant. Reale, which he co-owns with his sister Cristiana Romito, sits within a 16th-century monastery nestled in a remote medieval town in Abruzzo, Italy. As Niko Romito explained to Condé Nast Traveler, because of Reale’s remote location, tourists would often get there at the tail-end of a food tour of Italy—a tough situation to be in, when perhaps a meal at the end of a trip might feel less memorable after a string of stellar meals. “Today, it’s the exact opposite,” Romito said. “The location—tucked away in the provinces—was once a major limitation. Yet, this very constraint pushed me to create a style of cooking that transcends the distance, making the journey—the hours spent in the car—fully justified. I could say that the region where I live, Abruzzo, is beginning to emerge as a top destination for tourists. A territory rich in nature, parks, and hidden gems.”

At Singapore's Odette, number 15 on the list, Kampot Pepper Crusted Pigeon is served.

Inside Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Roye

Many restaurants within this year’s list support the growing trend that rurally set tasting menus are sometimes more interesting than their big-city counterparts, luring an increasing number of diners. This year’s number one restaurant and also the Best Restaurant in Europe is Asador Etxebarri, which calls Atxondo, a village of less than 1,500 inhabitants in Spain’s Basque Country, home. Vyn, the number 23 restaurant, is located within a pastoral fishing village of about 7,000 people in southern Sweden. While Naar, number 50 and also the winner for this year’s Sustainable Restaurant Award, sees diners traveling deep into the foothills of the Himalayas for its open-flame-cooked dishes. As food tourism continues to boom, expect even more meteoric restaurants to shine from beyond bustling metropolitan areas.
